SPRING WINDS. I heard the winds with unseen feet Pass up the long and weary street; They sang, "We come from hill and glen To touch the brows of toiling men, . "That each may know and feel we bring 'The first faint breathings of the spring, "To sweeten lane, and street, and square, And lighten all the dusty air. "The hills from which we come lie bright • In something of a richer light. "The long, deep glens and woodlands lie In softer shadows to the eye. "The birds have caught a finer note To throb with joy each feathered throat. "The streamlet echoes sweet and clear The liquid pulsing of the year; "rid everywhere you look is seen Life dawning in a tinge of green." Thus sang the winds as up the street They passed with heard, but unseen feet; And, as they went, a cloud above Sent downward tears of spring and love. --Good Words. A LMKANDEIt ANDERSON.

"I can never be more than a sister to you," said a buxom widow tenderly to an old bachelor who had pro- posed. " Ah, madame, yes. you can," he responded, gatlantle. "ram not a man to lose hope." 'Yes, but I say I -canna," she persisted. "You have daughters, madame," he said, "and you may yet be my mother-in- law." Sir George Rose was at a funeral on a Htterlv eeld day in winter, andhis companion In a mourning coach called his attention to the poor men in scarves, and bearing staves, who were trudging along by the side of the carriage. "Poor fellows !" said his companion, "they look As if they were frozen " Frozen!" retu , Sir George, "my dear friend, they are mutes,krtt I 'liquids.'" One day while Dr: B. W. Richardson was engaged at his house with an old patient who had been away many years in India, George Cruikshank's card was handed to the docfor. "It must be the grandson, or the son, at any rate, of the great artist I remember as a boy," said the patient. "It is impossible the George Cruikshank of Queen Caroline's trial time can be alive!" The doctor asked the vivacious George to come in. He tripped in,t in his eighty-fourth year: and when the old officer ex-i pressed.bia astonishment. George exclaimed, " show! you whether he is alive." With this he took the poker, and tongs from the grate, laid them upon the carpet, and; executed the sword dance before Dr. Richardson's as-. tonished patient. NOTHING CRAZY ABOUT Hem.—John Mc.Lennan, an impecunious citizen of Austin, VMS supposed to be crazy, and his relatives brought him beiore the county court to have a lunatic() inquirendo jury pass on his mental condition, his delusion being that he was very rich. A lawyer proceeded to ask the crazy man questions to test , his sanity. "I hear that you are going to build. a 50.000 dollars' fesidence?" "It is going to cost 60,000 dollars." "You don't say so!" "Yes, and lam going to start a daily paper with 250000 dollars' capital. That'i a mere trifle for a man of my means." "You seem to have so much money, perhaps you would not object to lending, me ten dollars?" "I'd like to do it, judge, but that would be such a risky investment everybody would . suspect me of being crazy." The refusal of the supposed lunatic to seriously entertain the idea of lending money to an Austin lawyer caused the jury to decide that Sam was in full possession of his reasoning faculties.-.- American- ELECTRICITY AS A MOTIVE POWER.--Me continually hear electricity spoken of as a •motive power, and ;the prediction is freely mite.° that it will soon take the plane of the steam engine; that it will be employed to propel vessele across the Atlantic, and the like. But such a view of 'the matter is wholly without scientific basis. Electricity, in its important applications to machinery, is never in WWII a source of power. It is merely a con- venietit and easily manageable form of energy, by which mechanical power is transferable from an ordinary prime motor, as a steam engine or a water-wheel, to a secondary motor which is employed to do the work. It performs an office precisely analagrus to that of a belt or line Of shafting, which, however useful in conveying power from one point to another, can, under no conceivable circumstances, be capable of otiginating it. It would be aimost impossible to catalogue the number and variety of purposes fbr which the electric motor is now in ,dally use. Some of the most usual applications are for printing presses. sewing machines„ elevators, ventilating fans, and machinist's lathes. ,At the present time every indication unmistakably points to the probabilty that within a very few years nearly all mechanical work in I large cities, especially in cases in which the power re- quired does not exceed, say, 50 horse-power, will be per- formed by the agency of the electric motor. It is an ideal motor, absolutely free from vibration or noise, perfectly manageable, entirely safe, and with the most ordinary care seldom, if over, gets out of order. Indeed, there is no reason totuppose that the limit of 50 horse- power will not be very largely exceeded within a coin- . paratively short period, when it is remembered that acarceTy five years ago the production of a successful 10 horse-power motor was considered quite a noteworthy achievement—Seribner's Magazine. Tux MORTALITY OF MODERATE DRINICING.—SOTOS, light is thrown on the vexed question of the superior healthfulness of abstinence or moderate drink- ing by recently published returns. The United King- dom Temperance and General Provident Institution has two sections of lives. The one section consists of abstainers only. The other of non-abstainers, known drunkards being excluded. During the period of 21 years the number of expected deaths in the moderation section was 5,785. Only 184, fewer deaths actually oscurred. The expectancy among the abstaining assured was 3,655, and the deaths amounted to 1,076 less. There is, therefore, the enormous deficiency in favour of teetotal survivors beyond expectancy of fully 26 per cent. The teetotal assured have received bonuses, on an average. 24. per cent, higher than have accrued to the restricted drinkers. Authentic returns of the time during which members of friendly societies have received benefit tend to show the comparative freedom from incapacitating illness of nephalists. The " Rechabite Directory" 'for 1887-8 gives some interesting comparisons. Between 20 • and eo years of age the Salford Unity of Rechabites (all abstainers) show only 48 weeks, as against 59.6 weeks of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows, a superiority of 11.6 weeks. Between 60 and 70 years the Rechabites had 501 weeks to 62'5 weeks of the Oddfellows, a difference of 124 weeks. Grouping these figures tokether, the Rechabites had 98'1 weeks, as against 1221 Weeks of the Oddfellows, a gain of 24 weeks. The abstaining followers of the son of Rechab come out also well compared with the' Foresters. From 20 to 70 years of age they Suffered from 98 weeks of ill-health, as Opposed to 1263 weeks among the Ancient Order of Foresters; between 70 and 80 years, from 122 weeks as opposed to 148-2 weeks among the Foresters. Collecting these returns together, the Rechabites required financial benefits during 220 weeks, and the Foresters during 2745 weeks, a difference in favour of the Rechabites of

54-.5- weeks.' There can be naledoubt-as to the general r • tendency of these striking tables in favour of the health- fulness of abstaining temperance.—'British Medical Journal. A VISIT yo Lztort Ilmrr.—We forgot the tea-table and forgot the hours, while he introduced us to his daughters, to his flowers (he called them "his gentle household ' pets"), and to his latest lit rary interests and occnpa- - tions. He wore the dignity and sweetness of a man not only independent of worldly ambitions, but of one dependent upon unworldly satisfactions. There was no sense of defeat because he was a poor man, nor even of inadequacy, except for lack of time and strength to entertain strangers." He wore the air of a noble labourer—ceaseless, indefatigable; and when we remem- ber that the wolf was driven from his door through so long a life by his busy pen, a pen unarmed with popular force, he might well feel that the struggle had been an honourable one. In referring to his flowers, which were just breaking into clusters of bloom, he fell into a reverie in talk upon the mystery and ministry of beauty in the world, a subject which he has made peculiarly his own ; but he soon strayed into the beloved paths of literature, and then indeed everything else .was forgotten. His daugh- ters tried in every way to decoy him to the table, but in vain, until at length they ran off with half his audience, when he soon followed: Wheretver Hunt lived, flowers - seem to have been his inseparable companions. Even in . those younger days in prison, he papered his walls with a trtilis-of roses, and caused plants to be put before the barred windows. They were as characteristic com- panions as his books. It seemed the most natural thing possible to hear Leigh Hunt talk of Shelley and Keats as lf they had just closed the door by whiCh we had entered. . There was the very couch, perhaps, where Keats lay down to sleep, after, as he says, straying in "Spenser's halls ;" for they had no room for hire we remember, and ii he was made to rest the among th, , ooks; and there, 1 , •,,,,,. 1 ' when he awoke, were • Might half slumb'ring on his nwri right arm. div.head: OUR LONDON LETIER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETIER

LONDON. THURSDAY NIGHT. i It is many Years since the House of Commons bounded parated for the Easter recess with such well- anted satisfaction. The section of the session by Easter has been put to admirable uses. )IDne important measure, the Conversion of the National Debt Bill, has actually passed through all its stages, and received the Royal assent. Another great scheme, Mr. Ritchie's Bill of Local Govern- ment, is fairly before the House; and last; though not least, among ministerial achievements, the Buds et Speech has been delivered. This is an event ithat has taken place very nearly four week.s beford it was reached last session. In 1887 the Budget fwas not reached 'till the 21st April, nearly a fort-, night after the House had returned Ifroin its mock; ery of an Easter Holiday. In addition to this for- ward state,of Ministerial business, private members have this year re-established their rights to assume Isome initiation of legislation. Mr. Bradlaugh alone claims two conspicuous successes—one, the Second reading of the Oaths Bill, and the other, the ap- pointment of a Committee which will undoubtedly sign the death warrant of the infamous system of pensions which has so long grown fat at the expense of the British tax-payer. Another important step has been the appointment of a Select Committee to inquire into the departmental administration of the Army and Navy, and another to investigate the pro- cedure in preparing and voting the Estimates. For this new and happy order of things, Mr. Glad- stone is personallYresponsible. He kis assumed an attitude of something more than benevelent neutrality towards the Goyernment. He is in fact their protector, standing between them and any tendency towards unnecessary cavilling that may manifest itself on the Opposition Benches. ,Of course, the particular character of the measures in- troduced by the Government have something to do with the birth of these halcyon days; but it is that character that makes it possible for Mr. Gladstone and the Opposition to assume theirliresent attitude. What the Conservative gentlemen now in ode habitually do is to treat as their, own own a policy originally advocated by the Liberals when in office, and then violently opposed by its present adopted parents. That is literally the case in respect of the Rules of Procedure. How in.lBBl the Tories fought this question, which they have now carried with a rush is within everyone's recollection. Their great scheme of Local Government Reform is so essen- tially radical, and in ' all its broad lines 'so closely, follows upon the Liberal Bill of 1882-3 that Mr. Gladstone could do nothing else than take the familiar bantling ' to his am. As for the Budget, one of Mr. Gladstone's Most promising pupils is in charge of Conservative finance, and naturally enough, it takes on a Liberal complexion. What is happening now in British home politics is that, as the only means of retain- ing office, the Conservatives are carrying out a Liberal policy, and though the personal arrange- ment is unusual and can he only temporary, it is not for Liberals to quarrel with the nett results. Shortly after the House meets again a.cloud, at pre- sent no bigger than a man's band, is likely to over- spread the summer skies that now:smile over the House of Commons. At Mr. Gladaone's instance great efforts were made to preserve the privacy of the meeting of Liberal leaders held at Earl Spencer's house on Tuesday. The übiquitous Press Associa- tion nevertheless issued an account of the proceed- ings, which indicated that the business of the meet- ing was confined to discussion of the Local Govern- ment Bill.. I have good reason to know that that, was only one half, and the least important part of the story. The attitude of Mr. Gladsterfe and his friends towards.the Local• Government Bill is no secret. It has . been proclaimed in several state- ments made in the House•.of Commons, thelatest by Mr. Gladstone on the very eve of the adjOtirn- meat for the holidays. One other, and from a political point of view, a more important topic of discussion was the. Budget. A good many serious holes were picked in it, and • when the,committee, stage is reached somedamaginz attacks-Will be made • . from the front Opposition bench. • Yet another old style member of the Hpuse of Commons has gone over to the majority. 'This is Mr. George Storer, whose name will not he familiar to the public, though he sat for South Nottingham' for eleven years, and had some position in the House as an authority on agricultural matters. How, this was gained is not very clear. Certainly it was not by the delivery of articulate speech. Mr. Storer was one of the gentlemen whom the House of Commons in its riotous moods used to delight to poke fun at. Mr. Storer was a short, spare, elderly gentleman, who in the Parliament of 1880 sat on the third bench behind the Conservative leaders. During one of the all-night sittings in the session of 1881 Mr. Storer unexpectedly rose and showed signs of intention to deliver a speech. For all the House knew it was his maiden speech, and that he should select this hour for delivering it passed corn- prehension. A sudden sharp roar of angry remon- strance went forth, which so terrified Mr. Storer that he immediately resumed his seat without com- pleting a sentence. Always after that, on the rare occasions when he tried to speak, the House humour- ously roared at him, keeping up the shouting as•long as he remained on his feet, which was never very
.h,armas.

long. Mr. Herbert Gardner, member for the Saffron Wal- den Division of Essex, has done a good deal to in- troducesometbing new-in the dinner giving line. One of the principal features in a successful dinner is the precise number present. Sir Henry Thomp- son religiously observes the perfect number eight. His dinners are always "octaves,' and his guests carefully selected for conversational purposes. Whilst eight is the perfect number, ten shas its re- commendations as providing for accidents. If from an accepted number of ten one or even two may at the last moment be prevented from putting in an appearance, the meeting is not fatally injured. Moreover, as far as trouble and expense- are con- cerned, one dinner of twenty-four is not equal to two dinners of eight. Twelve at table runs the

success of the dinner dangerously close. But if twelve is once passed, what should be a cosy din- ner party becomes a table d'hôte assembly, conversa- tion being almost necessarily confined to the neigh- bour right or left. The touch and go of generil conversation, one of the choicest treats where there are witty men and fair women, is absolutely lost. Still. *here a man has a very large circlrof ac- quaintances and plenty of Money and opportunity. life is not long enough to go on giving dinners of eight or ten. The other night Mr. Herbert Gardner had forty guests at dinner, chiefly Parliament men from Lords and Commons. To seat them at one long table, ac- cording to the ordinary fashion, would have re- embled the muster on board a P and 0 steamer at six in the evening, or the table &hots in a fashionable hotel. To avoid this Mr. Gardner had eight tables, seven holding either four or five, and one in the centre of the room seated for six. There were no names ticketed, but the•large party gradually broke up into groups, and sat down at any table near which they chanced to find themselves. The tables being close together twe or three groups occasion- ally lapsed into general conversation. One other convenience of tile arrangement is that there is no waitilig for guests who may turn up late with the weary excuse that they were kept for a division. Dinner is served at eight. Those present sit down, and any late comers may drop into any vacant place without causing disturbance or bringing a blush to his own forehead. There is a noble lord on the Conservative side who gives frequent dinners on the same plan, picking up men at the House or the club. At these modern dinners evening dress is not de riguer, the convenient principle underlying all the arrangements being that the whole thing is as impromptu as Mr. Wemmick's marriage ceremony. I met the other night a man whose name was once in 'everybody's mouth, but who is now so entirely—forgotten that -one is amazed to find he t3till presumes to live:. It was • Paul du Chaillu, whose adventures. in Equatorial Africa twenty- seven years ago convulsed the World, and led to -a controversy for a parallel to which we must look to what took place when Darwin's famous book was published. The amazing thing was to find the discoverer of the gorilla still in the prime of life. He is, I should guess, only just turned fifty, and must have been a more stripling when he„made the acquaintance of our great ancestor. After the pub- lication of 4is famous work, M. du Chtullu spent a good deal of' time in the United States, where he made much money as a lecturer. He has now settled down in London, living within measurable distance of the. ZoOlogical Oardone, Bit I gather that his travelling days will not hereafter xtend beyond the limits of that interesting locality. Recently Mark Twain contributed to one of the American magazines a charming paper, in which he collated specimens of the sort of answers which school children give in their exercises. A well- known school inspector has a story which shows • that the English boy is in this respect at least equal ; to his American cousin. One such was instructed to set forth in writing his views of the constitution of the human body. Here is his reply, which really seems too good to be true :—" The human bodyas made up of the head. the thorax, and the abdomen. , The head contains the brains, when there is any, The thorax contains the 'heart, lungs, and diafram: The abdomen contains thig bowels, of which there . are five, a, e, i, o, u, and adinatimed,* and

Next .TUe'sday. is Mr. Henry Richard's birthday, and many people who knoVehim will be surprised to learn that he is only four years off four score. He is three years Mr. Gllacistone's junior. and is one of the very; few; ;septuagenarians who can compete with Ithe ‘44-Prernier in the matter of apparent virility. Looking at the er for Merthyr, an observer woula, in spite venerible hirsute ap- panages, be inclined ess that he was nearer sixty than seventy. Mr. Richard, like other private members has for many sessions retired from that position of prominence he once occupied. But under this New Rules, and the happier auspices of the hour, private members are coming into their own , again, and the member for Merthyr may renew his Parliamentary youth like the eagle. 1

div.head: WELSH CONCERT AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: WELSH CONCERT AT WARRINGTON.

• On Monday evening a concert, promoted by the Welsh residents of Warrington, was held at the Co- operative Hall. , There was a large and appregiative audience, and the concert was, in every way a success. The chair was occupied by 'Alderman 'John Crosfield, J.P., who, in the course of a few opening remarks, said that he was pleased and sUrprised to see that there were such a number of Welsh people in Warrington as were assembled there that night, that was, if they were all Welsh: Ile was very fond of the Welsh people. In the first place they were all very good liberals, and that suited him. (Cheers). They were in favour of justice to Ireland, and out of 32 members of Parliament 30 of them supported Mr. Gladstone and his policy. That was a pretty fair majority for Wales. There was another reason why he liked the Welsh. They were in. favour of disestablishment. (Cheers). He was strongly in favour of disestablishment, because he believed that it would do more good to the Church of ngland, and to religion generally, than anything else would. There was a great deal of bigotry and superstition that wanted doing away with, and he thought that dise,sta.blishment would go a great way towards attaining that object. The Other evening he took the chair at a Bible meeting, held in connection with the British and Foreign Bible Society, in a small village not far from Warrington. The clergyman who had the control of the church schoolroom was asked if he would allow the meeting to be held there, but he would not. Therefore they had to hold a meeting in the Wesleyan chapel. They invited a clergyman in the neighbourhood to attend the meeting, and he replied, "'{o; I am not going to attend a meeting in a Wesleyan chapel." He said that he would attend if the meeting was held in the Church schoolroom, but the other clergy- man would not allow that. It was such a state of things that he wanted to see remloved in this country. He wanted to see the clergy of the Church of England and Dissenting ministers brought closer to each other. He• did not himself see that a clergyman of the Church of England was any better than a Dissenting minister, or that a Dissenting minister was any better than a Church of England clergyman. He hoped that before many years ha A passed they should see the Church disestab- lished, and they might depend upon it that the first part of the country where it vould be disestablished Would be Wales. 1 He hoped that those present would have a very pleasant —evening, and enjoy themselves. (Cheers.) The musical programme was then commenced by Miss K; Williams, who played a selection On the pianoforte; and Mr. D: Edwards followed with the song, "The diver," his rendering of which was much appreciated. Mrs. Henderson sang "Robin Adair," and, in response to an enthusiastic encore, she gave "Tapping at the gate." Mr. Pierce Hughes sang 'Alice, where art thou," and Miss K. Williams " Bwthyri bach Melyn," in such a manner as gained for them the hearty 'applause of the audience. A duet in Welsh, given by • Messrs. Hughes and Edwards, was also very well receteed. This con- cluded the first part of the programme. The second part commenced with the duet, " Larboard watch," which was well rendered by Messrs. Hughes and Edwards, and Miss K. Wijliams followed with the song, "The spirit of Spring" By desire' Mr. Hughes then sang "When other lips," and Mr. Edwards gave the "Vicar of Bray." . Mrs. Henderson was encored for her singing of "The Better Land," and responded with "The dream." The remaining items on the programme were the duet "Ex- celsior," by Messrs. Hughes and Edwards, the Welsh National Anthem, which was given by Mr. Hughes. The ' proceedings terminated with the singing of "God save the Queen." Miss Lizzie Owen, who had been announced to take part, was unable to be resent. Mr. Geo* Riley ably accompanied the singers on *the pianoforte. ,

div.head: SUNDAY TRADING AT WARRINGTON
div.p: SUNDAY TRADING AT WARRINGTON

• At the Borough Court at Warrington, on Monday, James bicelew, Horseraarket-street, was summoned for having, on the 11th and 18th days of March, ,unlawfully exercised his ordinary calling as a tobac- conist, the same nct being a work of necessity or charity. The days in question were Suudays.—ln answer to the_charge defendant said that he was guilty of selling on Sundays, but as he had done it for twenty odd years before and had not been in- terfered with, he thought it was rather strange that he should now be sturimoned.—Mr. J. L. Whittle (Deputy Town Clerk), who appeared to prosecute. said that as defendant roleaded guilty he was not desirous of saying anything in, reference to the case. —Mr. Hunt (the Chief Constable) : I should like to say a few words if Mr. Whittle does not.—Mr. Whittle : If you wish me to say something t will do so.—The Mayor (Alderman Sutton) : I think we should be in possession of some of the facts.—Mr. Whit- tle said the proceedings were instituted under an old Act of Parliament dating back to 1677—the time of Charles 11.—which Act provided for the keeping holy of the Lord's day. This Act set forth, amongst other things, that no tradesman should follow his calling on the Sab- bath, the sum of 5s being the penalty incurred thereby. The proceedings of that day were not taken exactlYin the spirit of the Act, and not entirely uponreligious grounds. He did not know that proceedings would have been taken at all, had it not been that several complaints had been made.—The Mayor: That is what we want to ar- rive at ; the ,reason of the prosecuqon.—Mr. Whittle: Thltre are a great many people who sell tobacco and cigars. (Mr. Hunt : And on a Sunday.) They are de- sirous that they should not open on a Sunday, but they say that if one person opens they are compelled to open. —Mr. Pierpoint asked if the complaint was made. by some interested person.—Mr. Whittle replied that the in- formation had been laid by the Chief Constable. Atten- tion had been called to the matter by a prominent mem- ber of the Town Council. Notice was then given to all the tobacconists who traded on Sundays, and, with thd exception of Mr. McClew, they ceased to do business on the &bbath.—The Mayor: We understand that, as far as this charge is concerned, it is entirely owing to the fact that other parties who do not sell on Sundays are not satisfied when Mr. McClew sells.—Mr. Whittle re- plied that practically that was so. If the Bench decided the case against the prosecution, the other shops would next Sunday be open.—Defendant said that the little trade he did on a Sunday helped him out in his income; he should not be able to pay his way without it. In answer to the Mayor, he said that only one shutter was left open.—The Mayor said that the Bench were bound to go by the Act of Parliament,which distinctly said that there should be no trading on Sun- days. At the same time they did not wish to inflict a heavy penalty. They should, therefore, simply impose the small fine of is, and they wished to say that not only the person who sold goods on a Sunday; but the people who came into their shops to purchase, were respon- sible under the Act, and were liable to a penalty.—The magistrates accordingly imposed a fine of is,' and costs in one case only; making 7s in all.

He (Mr.' Derbyshire) was of opinion that• the -questions in the books which the : doctor ought to give answers to ought not to be answered liehtly.—Mr. VOISEY said he agreed with Mr. Derbyshire that the answers ought not to be given lightly.—The CHAIRMAN said it was a matter Per the medical officer to reply to, and it :was agreed ti #t Dr. Spinks should be sent for.—The minutes of the Mita mitteowere then confirmed.—Later in the meeting Dr. Sprites aime into the Beard-room, and Mr. Derbyshire having repeated his remarks he said that he saw the man in question on the 14th, and passed him into the hospital, where he was put to bed. THE CHILDREN TO BB RE-VACCINATED. The Padgate School Committee's minutes stated that • the Medical Officer (Dr. Peacock) had reported the gene- ral health of the children to be excellent, and that he recommended that some of. the children be re-vaccinated, seeing that smallpox was threatening the neighbourhood. —The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that 'with regard 103 the vaccination -question the eommittee preferred that the Board should deal with the matter rather than that they should issue an order, as there were some members of the committee who felt very strongly on the subject.-'-Mr. JOLLEY seconded the pin- posal, and remarked that the proper thing to do. under the circumstances was to take the advice of their doctor. —Mr. Vomit's' though k it' was the duty of the Board to support' the medical offiCer.—Mr. GREENING said he understood the doctor reported that all children above ten years of age be re-vaccinated, and those under ten who did not show marks.—The CHAIRMAN : " SOlrkes in- cludes those.—The CLERK suggested that the doctor's advice should be acted upon, and if it was wrong the responsibility'rested upon the officer. If a medical officer advised them to do something and they did not do it they took upon themselves a very great responsibility.— The Cintioisau remarked. that the words of the doctor were—" Considering that small-pox is getting nearer to us every day, I think all our children in the schools over ten years of age should be re-vaccinated, and any under ten years not bearing good marks should be re-vaccinated also. DARBYSHIRE loolced upon that as a ,very im- portant matter. The doctor had used very vague terms; he said " I think" it better to do so and so, but hq did not recommend. The Board were not bound to carry out everything the doctor recommended; they could take the responsibility upon themselves if they wished, and there- .f ore he moved aSi an amendment that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of that referring to re- vaccination. He had neverrernembered a case of re-vac- cination being recominended by that Board, although the Board had always upheld the law that everyone Should be vaccinated. But re-vaccination was another question, and he thought there would be no harm in postponing consideration of that matter and so give every member of the Board an opportunity to be present when it came forward.—Mr. BLACEHITRST seconded this proposition. It was, he said, a serious thing for that Board to decide that morning, and was different from , that they had been in the habit of discussing. The , children were:all healthy, and why should they upset , them with re-vaccination ?—Mr. GREENING supported Mr. Derbyshire's amendment. He did not, he said, like to set himself up against a medical man as to what was good or what was bad for the human body, but he did think that was a piece of business that might be left over to a future time. He did not think it was neces- sary at all.—Mr. Ctaitaz supported the amendment. It would appear to him that that was more of a money question than anything else. ("No, no.") He was sorry to make those remarks but, he would quote the remarks • of Mr. Ritchie ot.july last year in the House of Com- mons. He said that since the system of rewards to vac- ' einators was adopted by Parliament the number of sue- eessful vaccinations had been nearly doubled. He , might also take other figures from the Local Government • Board which told him that every person vaccinated , in England and Wales cost 4s 6d.—Mr. Jottev supported the proposal of the doctor.—The CLEna said the doctor had made a recommendation, and had therein fulfilled his duty. If effect was not given to the recommenda- tion responsibility did not fall upon him. With regard to payment, there was a small fixed fee to the medical man upon a successful vaccination.—Mr. JOLLEY said it had been thrown put that it was a matter of money, but he did not think any such thought had ever entered Dr. Peacock's head. The children in the school were healthy, . and he wanted to keep them healthy.—Mr. GREENING said he never for one momont entertained the idea that • it was a money matter. If they came to that they got very low indeed. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. CLARICE explained • that he said it looked like a money question. 'Me gave the opinion of other men, and not his own. The doc- tor did not tell them that if the children were re-vacci- nated they would not haye small-pox provided it came ' Into the neighbourhood:—Mr. JOLLEY : He cannot; the 3 doctor is not infallible,—Mr. VOISEY said the question of ' vaccination and re-vaccination was one matter after all. • —Mr. GREENING said he did not believe this, that, Tid I the ether, but if they entertained the matter in that spirit it was no use having a medical officer at all. (Hear, hhar.) With regard to the insinuation that it was a matter of money, he did not 'believe it for a moment. Mr. Clarke on a former occasion had said a great deal ' about the bad effects that came from vaccination, and ' he (Mr. Voisey) would ask them to let him read about an investigation that had been made by inspectors of the • Local Government Board in fourteen cases where vaccination was supposed to have produced a very 3 injuriobs effect. The extract read as follows 3—' ' Investigation has been made by inspectors of the Board's ' medical department into 14 cases where vaccination was believed to have produced some injurious effect. The 3 'allegations of injury came from a variety of sources and were usually of a very ihdefinite character. -One of them proved to be an example of careless vaccination by ' a private practitioner, resulting in undue irritation of the arms of several children: The rest of the complaints referred to single children, and in tw6 of these instances only did there appear reason for connecting the child's ; complaint with its vaccination. One was the case ,of a , child whose arm had been dressed by the mother with 5 brown paper and cobbler's wax, and who got an axillary ' abscess in consequente ; another case was a slight erup-

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. OVID MATES. Hello! come in, un shut thad door. Wod ! Bobby! Is thad thee? Hey, bless tho ! ged Alf owd arm cheer, hile wi'

tin camp a while wi' me: Just reych tilled a pipe fro' th' rack; That's t' bacco-pot on theer ; dornd be feared on't, aveve some mooar On t' shelf ut back o'th' spier. Th' wife's gooan a longish errand, sooa • W•fll smook un rest eawrsels, Un Wlish th' hooatnly comfort, Bob, As brass ne'er gives to th' swells. We've hed eawr troubles thick, owd lad,i Bud fowt thro', fair un streyt ; Un Bob, we've ite'er rued tearftil eon Thro' doin' wed worn'd reight. Let's see! It's welly sixty year Sin' we wur mates ut fost tln yet tha'rt hearty, lithe, un cant, " Tbe,, tchiched ut th' top wi' frost. Th' world dashes on i' progress ruts, Ut Bitch a fearful rate, , It's left ifs like owd omanacks, Forgetten—eawt o' date! ` Aw've lattely thowt abeawt gwd times, When thee un me wur lads; • When th' lasses wore no humps, un kept . Their yure i' trim beawt pads. For.swaggerin', gawky fella-lads, Thr world hedn'd med mitch room, For then they hed to buckle to Ut weyvin' on th' hand-loom. Aw titter every time aw think O'er th' gam we used to hey; Tha knows we once took th' parson's gooat To th' barber's for a shave. We teed a big card reawnd id neck, • As read "Shave off mi beard," .Un then shoved Billy into th' shop— ' Hey wornd thad birber feard ! Un then as we grew owder, Luv Begun eawr hearts to swell,— Neaw, Bob, dornd look so rooagish, mon, Th' owd rigs awst never tell. Tha knows as t' laeses, thine un mine, Booath promised as they'd join Their lot wi' eawn, one moonleet fleet Up you Losgshaw Loyne: Heaw time's rolled on, id nobbUt seems - • A.s tho' twur yesterday, Sin, wi' eawr mates, i' th' Kitty fields, We used to romp un play. Bud when aw think ov out's passed Sin th' curls wur on ml heead,. Ther's automat heavy smites ml heart Un meks id feel like leod. Yet, Bobby, tha's bin true as steel, • Mi mate, thro' thick un thin; Thi ready band un heart unchanged . Thro' t' changes as ther's bin. Tha's toiled un browt thi famly! Un aw've done t' same wi' mine; There nooan aw like, beside mi own, As weel as thee 'un` thine ' • • God. bless you good owd wife o' thine, Un God bless mine un o ; They've cheered us welly fifty year, Thro' sunshine un thro' slum. • Let's o cling clooase together, till Earth's dust drops fro' eawr sboon ; Then When o's o'er, we'st happen be Owd mates i' th, land aboon.

, BY SEAN' 31IDDLEMASS, . Author of "-Ltuly Muriel's Secret," "The Spider and the Fly," " ppisoned Arrows," "Wild Georgie," &c., .&c. . • I
CHAPTEII XI. FERDINAND AT ROME.

"Handsome Ferdinand," as ibis a sort of fashion' to call the Stanhope's second son, is lying full length on the sofa in Mrs. Purvis's .room. , His hands are folded under his head, and there is a radiant look on his face which is scarcely in accordance with the agonised expression his countenance bore only two nights ago. Either he has played still higher and won back the heavy sums he had lost, or he has found softie Means. to pay his debts, 'for there S itO,sign of Mre sitting heavily on that curled brow; not even does his broken promises to his mother seem to rest on it. . With fortune once more at the prow has he entered with himself upon a fresh resolution to keep that promise in the future; or, as is Most probable with men of Ferdinand's temperament, has be altogether forgotten if for the time? Whatever the cause, he seems Satisfied, and content, and is apparently more' at his ease in Mrs. Purvia's room than in any other spot in the house. Geoffrey and Irene are in the painting room, Lady Fedora in the drawing-room, yet none of these even know that Ferdinand is not at Aldershot. It is a habit of ,his to one qoietly iiit the house, and, es it were,: take refuge in PuiVis's sitting-room He hears Much, more news there than hq, does upstairs, he says,; and not tin- frequently, he leaves the house again without even saying "how d'ye do?" to any member of his family. ~ Mrs. Purvis is sitting by the table, stile of linen and white work in front ,of her,on which to all intents and purposes she is busily engaged. Her eounten-", :ance beams with satisfaction, and she looks much ' oftener at Ferdinand than at the work. Cross Purvis is quite g different person when Ferdinand is With her;- and well may people say she, is deimted ••Se you had tea with • your nephew Chilton, di ~4•en ?I shall,be.jealous of this Chilton if you go there 'too often.. ;Having tea in a young man's roomis not right, Purvis, indeed it isn't, you'll be wanting- to come to mine next.", "Oh Mr, Ferdinand'!" "Are you going to leave all your money to this Chilton V' he asked after a short pause. "No, indeed I'm not, and you know it well enough; you, know as I'm saving every blessed imnny for you, every penny leastwise as you'll let me save. It is a shame, a burning shame, I take it, that the eldest son should have all the nuts with the kernels,.. and give the yonnger sons the empty ones to crack. "I say, Purvis, did You ever hear anyone say that Geoffrey is not the governor's eldest son ? " " Lor', bless you, Ferdinand, whatever are yon talking about? If Geoffrey isn't the eldest, whoever is, I'd like to know ? " "That, I thought, perhaps, you would be able to tell me." "Do you mean as there is some mistake, and you is the eldest after 'all? Why, there's two good years atween you. I ought to know, me as saw you born, all of you, even Irene, though that silly fool Hannah *night is first with her ladyship." "No, Purvis," answered Ferdinand, laughing. " I don't mean anything so absurd, but there is a title going about that the governor had a son before he married my mother." "Well, and suppose he had, he wouldn't interfere 'with either you or Geoffrey, most gentlemen has a few of they sort of sons." "Oh, Turyis, what shocking morality. But I didn't mean anything of that kind but a real bond fide eldest son." "You want me to believe as Mr. Btanhope was. married afore. It ain't true, Mr. Ferdinand, not a • word of it; . it, couldn't a'been without my knowin' and me livin' here all these years." • 'Ferdinand seemed highly .amused at the old woman's reason for the iiiipossibility of . this mar- riage, and said; laughingly, " Well, ;it does not matter much .to me, does it? since' I am not the . oldest ;" but if there is any truth in the tale it might astonish Geoff one ,of these days." 'There'll be a good maoy, things as will astonish the folks in this house afore they're mu& older, but it won't be no stray on turning up .to put Geoff's nose out of joint.' "Good gracioua,whatrdo von mean,wkat will it be?" and Ferdinand rolled lazily over on his side; the easier to survey his companion, whose little innuen- does about the family always amusecliiim. ," If you wac te makeiti more of your business to he with, your,brother and sister you'd knew:" - "rlicy' bore inte," h repli d, "I can't stal,u hat endless daubing and lecturing on colours and efieeti." " PerhaPs if -you had a model to your taste you'd daub too."- "Mighty powers! she's hitting at Phyllis. 'No, I don't think She's ,pretty, she's too ruddy to please ; b,it I believe Geoffrey admire her.". "And that's the cool way you take it. Do you think that Mr.' Stanhope and. Lady Fedora Will be ac indifferent when they 'hear they've got that stack- up Phyllis for a daughter-hi-law." "Geoff Marry, Phyllis ! Really, Purvis, you are too kilhqgly absurd to-day. Why, my infidel brother Would as soon think of cutting his throat as of com- mitting such a mortal sin as the perpetration of a me.salliance." "Would he ? Saints trip sometimes as well as sinners, and you'll live to find. it out." "Marry Phyllis ? " repeated Ferdinand, "Why it's worse than gambling. I'm sure you're wrong, Purvis. My brother admires her as a model, you know, but he'll never think of marrying her." Believe it or not as you like, but if you take my Lady Fedora, you'll put her On guard." At the mention of his mother Ferdinand's brow clouded over, and he said far more seriously, `,;.‘ My, mother has as many worries as she well knows how to bear. I'll not trouble her with this nonsense; but }the first time Geoff offends me—and heveryfrequently does—l'll hurl it wildly at his head. It might not be such a bad thing though if Geoff married Phyllis—. eh ? The governor would be sure to disinherit him." "He can't, the estate is entailed; you ought to know that by this time." "Well, if I promise not to tell the governor that lies spooney on Phyllis, I might get Geoff to help me some day when I'm in a mess ; there is always an advantage to be got out of a man that degrades hTm- self.

"'Are you in a ro?,ss now ? " " No, I don't exactly want, Geoff's help at this moment, but_" "Don't you never ask it. If it is a hundred you're wanting, come to me. I'd rather do any- thing than let the family name rrs soiled by a marriage with that there Phyllis Knight. "Unless I'm driven I don't supsase I shall trouble my head about the matter," answer t: Ferdinand, yawn- ing. "I don't much care vet anyone in the family does as long as I get wh...2 I want, and they leave me in peace." But this was not at all the so V sl thing that suited Mrs. Purvis, whose great objec.. a was t ) spite the Knights, at the same time that she served Tom Chilton. "Look you here," she said, "it will suit your ends best in every way if you get Geoffrey off this silly fancy for Phyllis." • , "How so "Well, my nephew, Chilton, wants to marry her, and if you can arrange it for him he'll be a much stauncher friend to you, and- come forward with a good bit more coin than ever Mr. Geoffrey will." "So he wants to buy Phyllis, does he ? " I Now this was exactly what Mts. Purvis knew that Tom Chilton would not do. Had he not told het that Phyllis must accept him of her own free will, without coercion of any sort. She had, hoWever, no inten- tion of heeding this chivalrous backwardness. of Tom's if it in any way interfered with her mode of carrying out the scheme she had in view. - "I don't say exactly as he'd buy her. 'Taint always spades as should be called spades, Mr. Ferdinand ; but if the 'coast is made clear this yere marriage would come about of itself like." "And Tom-Chilton will help me if I give him a: hand, to put it gegeelly." "Just so, Ire's7evoted to you any way, on my ac- count." "Glad to hear I have another friend in the world, a friend with a bit of Money, too. How much is he . , good for?" That depends on circumstances, I . fancy," answered 'Mrs. Purvis prudently. She felt sho dare not commit Tom Chilton too, far. "I should like to see, this fellow," remarked Ferdinand. . "That won't do no mortal good. You'd best leave him to me_; just Tou try. and stop this I'ere love-making ,of Geoffrey s, and I'll see as Tom sticks 1,33' You." "So he is very much in love with Phyllis, is lie? It will not be easy to make Geoffrey give up his fancy, if fancy there is existing: However, no time like the present. Not that I care one brass button for Tom Chilton's assistance. I only pretended to do so to humour yoti, 'old woman. -I have winged some

much higher game," and heiolled Off the sofa wne.c he was speaking and stood erect before her. "Whatever are you going to do 7" she asked, somewhat anxiously. "Going upstairs, orcourse, to see what all my dear relations are doing, and whether there is anyone who expects to be afresh one lurking about." "I shall see you again before you go?" .40,1itia4 "Well, yes—probably." • lef And out of the housekeeper's room Ferdinand sauntered whistling. He was bound for the painting- room, where he loteiyied .to cast a few innuendoes both on the subject of Phyllis and that yet darker one of a probable eldest son, who, if he turned up, would unseat. Geoffrey from his pinnacle of primogeni- ture. On the stairs he met Lady Fedora, who gave him a loving kiss and said she was glad to see-him looking so brisk'. ",When had be come up from Aldershot? Of course he 'would Ally to dine," et cetera, et cetera. The sight of his mother trouble & Ferdinand not a little, and he would most gladly have dispensed with the meeting just then ;and is to, dn- g in family conclave, he felt that would be quite mtMerable, so he pleaded the excuse of an engagement with a fellow( and got away 'froln her "maternal gushing "i (as he irreverently called Lady Fedora's expressions of love and interest) with as little delay as possible. On, up into the painting-rooin he went. Geoff and Irene were startled by his entrance, but Phyllis was not there. - " How is it neither of you two are out?" he asked. "It has turned so wet and cold. We were going to a garden party at Mrs. Malcolm' Vinner's, but mamma' thought the weather not fine enough. I am disgasted," cried "SO I suppose you expected he would be there." "What he ? " she blushed. ' "Oh, don't imagine that I'm 'not up in your love affairs. I am not quite out of the world., though I don't •come, here very often. I know all about them; 'both -yeur's ancl Geofrs. Ah, you may well celour up, old fellow; it is a terrible mistake. You all look upon me as the black sheep of the family ;• but I wouldn't do such a thing as that." • Geoffrey pretended not to understand.. If he were ashamed of his engagement to Phyllis when it was alluded to by Ferdinand, what Would he be when his father and mother founctit out ? It was the first time this feeling had eVer Conic to Hint, and if anyone had • snegested that it would do so he would have repudiated the suggestion with 'scorn. Nor did it last for more than a second or two. Still it was there latent. The discovery scarcely contributed to his happiness, and irritated him socordingly., answered Ferdinand very, testily. "I. don't think .1 interfere muchwith your miserable gambling performances.. You Might by the same rule to let my affairs alone." • An angry Rush rose to Ferdinand's cheek. "If we were-more'like brothets weshonla be the better - able to stand together when the worst comes," he retorted. "The worst! What worst? -Mat there are diffi- culties I know, but they are of your making, Ferdi- nand. Our lathe is involve ol felt you.' When I come into the estates they will be free. Never' for a moment deceive yourself into imagining that I shall give up any of my rights to meet the. difficulties you incur by your own fault." "Your rights—your estates! Don't be so test, Geoffrey; Stop till y9u possess therm .Something you little expect may start up to stopithis swagger." "Nothing but my death can prevent. me, frora taking estates that are entailed." Suppose. the governor has an elder son knocking about in seme unknowq part of the world, where would you he then ?" • • Geoffrey looked aghast,. bet Irene set up a ringing peal of laughter. You always were imaginative, Ferdinand • but really, if you cannot invent a better tale than that to tease Geoff with, your intellect must be failing you." "Don't be pert, little sister. There may be more truth in this than you think for. I-don't say it is true, but that I have heard it, that's all."; "From some madman in his cups," said Geoffrey, angrily. "I advise you not to repeat it, Ferdinand;. casting such a slur on the reputktion of a Man like our father is scarcely fitting in one of his sons." "High horse, eh ? That's what you mean to ride, is it? Well, it will conic down to a pony or a jackass when 'the truth is proved, and you marry Phyllis Knight. Ta, ta,l muSt be off. I want to catch a train." Another' moment and he was gone, liskinwsown seed -which would agitate the earth on which it , had been cast for many a long day to come. Even Mrs. Purvis, downstairs in the offices, was sitting pondering over Ferdinand's strange tale • no wonder, then, that Geoffrey painted no more aftf;r Ferdinand left, but tliiimicrig --himself on a 'chair looked very' • dejected and white. Irene came and sat ens, footstool beside him. " is not true, Geoff. It is not true. You surely are not .going to worry about such nonsense as that ?" "true," and lie latigh4d ; "you don't suppose .1 think-there is any truth in such a report? but I are vexed, deeply vexed, because I am afraid. Ferdinand has got up this story in order to raise money." "How can he raise money 'by such means?" "I scarcely know ; thank Heaven, soy brain cannot followvll the entanglements in which Ferdinand in- dulges. Perhaps helms started soma:me he wants to palm off ,as my father's legitimate son." "But papa is alive •he knows. Let us telt him all about it ; or, better still, tell mamma." "Not for worlds" Irene, not for worlds. You do not understand—hot,/ should you ?—all the mischief which speaking of this subject will do. Promise me you will never mention "I promise, of course, Geoff, if you wish it; .but cannot see the good of silence since F‘rdinand is sure to say all that pleases him. He won't spare „anyone if it suits his purpose to be disagreeable. And she was right. It was Ferdinand Stanhope'e plan of life to treat everyone, whether relations a not, as mere machines invented for his conven?ence.. (To be continued.)

EVACUATION OF THE NEW HEBRIDES BY THE - FRENCH. SYDNEY, MONDAY.—lntelligence has been received here . announcing that the evacuation of the New Hebrides by e french troops is now 'complete, the troops having been transferred to Noumea. GENERAL BOULANGER. PARIS, MONDAY.—General Boulanger appeared before the Court-martial at the Eeole Militaire this morning, the hearing of hiS explanation only occupying ten minutes. After his departure the Court gave its deci- -sion, which will not be made known until after it has been communicated to President Cainot. On leaving the court General Boulanger proceeded to the residence of M. Laguerre. THE SENTENCE ON M. WILSON REVERSED. PARIS, MONDAY.—The Court of ' Appeal to-day gave judgment reversing the sentence passed by the Correc- tional Tribunal upon M. Wilson and other personi charged with being implicated in the decoration scandal; and ac- quitted all the accused. The judgment, while severely • condemning the acts imputed to M.Wilson and the Other defendants, declares that the offences with which they are charged do not fall under the application of. any ex- isting law. • GERMANY : THE EMPEROR FREDERICK. BERLIN,MONDAY.—IL is now decided that the Em- peror FrAerick shall proceed to Potsdam next month. The 'mpirial order that the usual spring review of the Guards shall be discontinued has given great satofaction in military circles. The "North German Gazette" learns that the Em- peror's sleep test night was at times interrupted by coughing, but that the expectoration has diminished. His medical advisers anxiously await the setting in of - milder weather in order that the Emperor may ,be able to enjoy some fresh air, weich he greatly misses at present. BERLIN, TEDRSDAY.—The Emperor Frederick, accorti- , panied by the Empress, took a driver for three-quartets ! of an hour this morning. Thd weather was beautiful, and the excursion, like yesterday's walk, has greatly benefited his Majesty. The Court will remain at Char- lottenberg till the end of April and then remove to Pots- dam, where the marriage of the Emperor's seciond son, Prince Henry, with his cousin, Princess Irene iz4 Hesse is expected to take place on the2nd May. ITALY AND ABYSSINIA. • Roma, Snwpat.—A despatch from Massowah of to- (lay's date announces that Ras Alula reached Ghinda at noon yesterday with Has Agos. Another Abyssinian column is reported to be Marching towards Ardereso under the command of Has Area Sa- lassie. eThe Negus is at Aznefas: These movements are . regarded as pointing to the probability of an early attack by the Abyssinians. THE RECEPTION OF QUEEN VICTORIA IN ITALY_ FLORENCE, SATURDAY.—No foreign sovereign has ever •' had a more enthusiastic reception, in Italy than that which greeted Queen Victoria on ' arrivine here yester- day. From an early hour the streets were crowded, and . ~ the houses and shVs were profusely decorated with Eng- , lish and 'ltalian flags. lathe Piazza del Duorno San Marco • two bands were stationed, which, on the arrival of the Queen's carriage struck up "God save the Queen." Her Majesty during the drive was evidently pleasedwith and gracious' acknowledged the splendid reception. Out- side the Porta San Gallo the erowds were very large, in- cluding not only peasants but the ladies and gentlemen • of the neighbouring villas. • ROAM, MONDAY N.DailT.—ln connection with the visit of the Queen to Florence a review of English and Italian warships on a somewhat extensive scale will be held at Livorno (Leghorn); at which her Majesty has consented to be present. . GREAT FLOODS IN THE ELBE VALLEY. &me, Mormee.—ln consequence of the bursting of ' a dyke the Nogat has overflowed its banks, submerging the low.lying district around for a distance of two Ger- man mile.' The inhabitants are taking refuge in this town, the suburbs of which are flooded. Intelligence from Dantzic states that before the dyke burst ice had accumulated below Marienburg, inconsequence of which a large part of the latter town was inundated and the 5,g1 inhabitants placed in imminent danger. The inmates of vee: the prison had to be rescued by the fire brigade. At the tosi Nogat mouth •of the Vistula eight villages are under water. Several houses have fallen and a large number of cattle have been drowned. "A HUNDRED VILLAGES UNDER WATER." < CASSEL, TllESDAY.—Appalling accounts are being re- ceived here of the inundations caused in the Elbe di/strict by the accumelatfon of ice and the consequent breaches made in the river banks. From Wittenberg to Dennen- berg and Boizerberg both banks of the Elbe are flooded for miles. A hundred villages are uncldr water, and • there has been some loss of life. The damage done is enormous and the distress terrible. Many cattle have been drowned. • STORM& IN NORTH AMERICA.—A TOWN t DESTROYED. • • New YORK, TURSDAY.—lntelligence from the North- 'western States announces that, terrific gales prevail in .hat region, causing great damage. The town of Nin- nescah, in Kansas, has been completely destroyed, three Persons being killed and seventeen_ injured. Severe sleet and snow storms prevail in the Lake region. -

HOUSE OF' COMMONS.--‘4OIIDAY. The Speaker rook the chair at three o'clock. Flees IN THEATitES.—MT. HARTLAND asked the Home Secretary whether, having rega.r& to the d trucden. of another theatre by fire at °ponce where a post 'number of lives had been lost, he could state when I was the ire tendon of the Government to introduce their Theatres Bill P—Mr. MATTHEWS : The Government have deoided riot to introduce a bill on. this subject. —Mr. HARTLAND : Will the Government no longer e,ontinare to block my bill P—Mr. IVierrnews : I can give no undertaking on that subject to my bon. fries& 'CRUELTIES ' OF RABBIT CoURSING.—MT. BtfeRAPTAN asked the Home Cemetery whether his attentionhad been called to the alleged cruelties at so-called "rabbit cours- ing" matches im enclosed spaces ?—hlr. MArrnews said the decisions of the Cont'of Queen's Bench e.srtainly alp, peered to show thaetheatts alleged were not an inf ring. , meat of the statute tor the prevention of ,cruelty to animals. /t was a matter for cessideration whether the law could ire amended, but in the meantime he hoped public opirijon would be strongenough to check practices I which 'meld not byeny stretch of language beconsidMed; spert. (Cheers.) i RATLWAY RATHS.—Mr. Suva, in reply to Mr. Chane rain, said the Railway Rates Bill would not be taken untilaiter the Local Government Bill'had been read •a seconddme. THE MUDGE/. INCREASED' REVESUE. , 111.01SES, VEHICLES. SECURITIES, AND CHOICE • WINES TAXED. REDUCTION DP THE INCOME TAX... , The House having game into Committee of Warps and Means, Mn. Courtney in the chair, ' Mr. GOSCHEN rose at half-pasfour to commence his .Budget speech, and concluded at a quarter to eight, the longest epeech, as it was the most prosperous 'Budget, for many year. Mr. Goschen commenced in the con- gratulatory mood, dwelling on thefact that there had been no supplementary estimates for the Navy, a happy event that had not taken place since 1876. Moreover, there were no supplementary estimates for the revenue departments, whilst the Civil 'Service estimates had been smaller than at any period for twenty years. In sup- poreof this good fortune there followedthe donble event, that whilst the expenditure had fallen short of the original estimates the revenue had considerably increased. The estimate for the Customs revenue and the yield had been remarkably level, a fact on which Mr. Goschen based a generous tribute to the prescience and abilities of the Civil Servants responsible for the work. Tea was fairly but not remarkably progressive I coffee was staL tionary ; tobacco natually showed 'a diminution of revenue consequent upon the reduction of the duty. But that Mr. Goschen explained was due to the fact that what he called „" the watering clauses" had not ,been in operation throughout the year. They were now in full swing, with the 'effect that every pipeful that was smoked yielded less ' vapour to the operator and more revenue to the State. The decline 'in the revenue from drink had et last been arrested, a fact in respect of which Mr. Gesehen's satisfaction as Chancellor of the Exchequer was temiStred by his regrets as a Moralist. The prineipal increase in consumption, and in consequent revenue, was in beer, which had been exceptionally Con- sumed during 'the Jubilee festivities. The increase of the drinlerevenue was £300,000. Stamps had also in- creased, chiefly in respect of the Death Dudes, which had benefitted by probate duty paid upon two estates contributing between them £lBO,OOO. Income tax was on 'the whole stationary. with a tendency towards decrease iri the , yield on the penny. As the 'result of a resume of the variations in the revenue as compared with the expenditure. Mr.' Goschen had to annpunce a realised eurplus of £2,165;000, which, be remarked amid cheers, was the largest sum recorded since the year 18734—that being, it may he ob- served, though Mr. Goschen did not mention it, the last financial yeer of Mr. Gladstone's Administration preced- ing the Conservative re-action. In addition to this pros- perous state of the balance sheet, ,Mr.. Goschen had the satisfaction of announcing that the effect • of the year's finance on the National Debt had been, the largest pay- ment since the ever prosperousepochalreadyalludedto, a triumph which Mr. Gladstone courteously acknow- ledged. Passing to the coming year, Mr. Goschen esti- mated an expenditure of £86,910,000, a diminution of £512,000, as compared with the actual expenditure of the current year. - Here the Chancellor of the Exchequer made one of numerous digressions, explaining the seitemeby which what he called the Imperial Defence Bills for the Army and Navy would be met, the first by an annuity scheme, and the second by manipulation 'of the Suez Canal funds, neither imposing fresh burd . upon the taxpayer. The.revenue for the coming year he estimated at £89,287,000, being £302,000 less thanthe actual receipts of the current year. He reckoned that on the basis of existing taxation he would have a surplus of £2,377,000. This was a conclusion loudly cheeredby the House. But the exultation was tempered by Mr. Goschen's admission that the demands of the President of the Local Government Board, in comtection with his new scheme, worked havoc and destruction with this handsome surplus. As Mr. Ritchie had stated, the grants-in-aid to the amount of £2,600,000, would be withdrawn. But there was imposed upon the Chancel- lor of the Exchequer the promise and the necessity of ex- tending a new grant in. relief of local taxation over and above the deduction amounting to £2,900,000, which more than swept away the surplus. Mr. Ritchie had promised "an important contribution "in the way of personalty. The desired object was to get at realised personal property, and this the Chancellor proposed to do by giving up to the local authorities one-half of the pro- bate duty. This important declaration was received without evidence of emotion by the House, an unexpec- ted consequence that evidently discomposed the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer. After A brief and unavailing pause for the cheers that should have come in, he 'went on to plead that the probate duty was a growing tax calculated regularly to increase in its mission of relief. A proposal to describe the new licenses to be'handed over to the local authorities awakened attention to what had grown to be a somewhat trying speech. Putting the cart before the horse, as he admitted in response to a remark made sotto vice from the front Opposition bench, Mr. Goschen dealt with the proposed new licences for ve- hicles. Starting from the premise that all who use the roads should pay for them,he proposed a tax of £1 for every vehicle exceeding 10 cwt. in weight, - with the excep- tion of agricultural carts, and 2s;6d. a wheel upon all vehicles over 2 cwt. Heavy carts and brewers' waggons he specially mentioned, amid general approval, would I bear both the tax for weight an the tax for wheels, the revenue under this head amounting to £300,000, A. voice suggesting "bicycles and tricycles," Mr. Goschen declared with emphasis that they would not be included in the tax. He also proposed to renew the old tax on horses—ll, upon all pleasure horses excluding trade 'horses, £5 upon racehorses (at which there was an ex- ceptionally loud cheer), horse dealers paying a eompo- eition of £l5. This would yield £540,000. There were some small remissions, touching'carriage duties, Sche- dule A of the income tax, and the tax on hawkers, which dater was altogether abolished. Summing, up the re- ductions, abolitions and increases, the CHANCELLOR of the E:xamenertldatd himself, after speaking two hours and a half, with a surplus which,' making provision for carrying over a balance, amounted to only £1,000,000. That was evidently not enough for a remission of a penny on the income tax, which required the sum of £1,555,000 An earlier of many digressive passages in the course of the speech had disclosed the right hon. gentlen's strong desire to reduce the income tax, and this dTclo- sure of only a million in hand left the House in some per*xity. But Mr. Goschen had not yet nearly finished. How was he to make up the something more than a mil- lion and a half necessary to reduce the income tax? A reference to revolvers led him off into still one other di- gression, in the course of which the House learned that •it is intended presently to introduce, a Bill dealing with revolvers, but rather from a police point of view than for revenue purposes. At length, and still reluctantly, the Chancellor of the Exchequer concluded his long sum of addition and subtraction. The £50,000 he would make lip out of additions to revenue in the matter of stamping deeds, and the other half a million out of a tax of ss. per dozen on foreign bottled wines, a companies re: gistration fee, and a stamp upon foreign secenties, the last a proposal which vied with the impost on racehorses as most successful in raising the enthusiasm of a heavily- weighted House. Some conversation followed, in which Mr. Childers and Sir William Harcourt took part. There was a general disposition favourably to accept the Budget scheme, whilst reserving liberty of discussion in details. With this object the resolution affecting the duty on foreign bottled wines having been agreed to, progress was .ree ported on the ordinary resolution on the Tea Duty, with the avowed purpose of affording the Committee a full opportunity of discus Sing the Measure. RESPITE OF A MURDERESS : EXTRAORDINARY SUICIDE.— The resOte of the Cardiff murderess has been followed by an extraordinary sequel. There was quite a difference of opinion in Cardiff as to whether she would be hanged or not, and a local showman made a heavy bet that she would be hanged. When he heard she was respited, he Committed suicide. IRISH EXHISITION LONDON.—PeThapS no exhibition of recent years is likely to give results, more practically useful, than the one which is to be opened early in the coming summer at Olympia, Kensington. Ireland pos- sesses great natural resources and important industries, , and a comprehensive display of What she can produce or manufacture will net only be an object lesson of the greatest interest to the people of Great Britain, but will do mueh to assist the revkal of trade in Ireland. The Exhibition is begun under the happiest auspices. knows neither politics, religion; nor class, but has for its Executive Council and Patrons the most distinguished representative men. Perhaps for no other purpose could nearly. 700 names, representing every phase of political, religious and social life, be brought together in active nnioti Tax Molex BRETTON TEAGEDY.—The terrible crime committed some weeks ago at Monk Bretton bya surgeon named Burke was investigated at Barnsley on Monday,. when the accused was for the first time able to appear in court. The prisoner, it may be remembered, wound up a drinking bout by shooting his little daughter, a'girl of nine, for whom, according to one witness he had an affection almost approaching idolatry. Burke was now .only a wreck of his former self. To show his animus and his mental condition at the time, a letter was now put in which the prisoner wrote for his wife's reading shortly before the lamentable affair. In this he Said that he at one time loved her (Mrs. Burke) hard, but she had "completely converted this into entire indifference." Prisoner's counsel said the defence was that the' revolver went off by accident, and that the prisoner's attempt at suicide was the result of his horror at whathad happened. The prisoner was committed for trial. MURDER NEAR YEOVIL.—On Saturday morning, Martha Charles, said to be atrout 50 years old, was found mur- dered in a house at illimbrook, near Yeovil. The dwel- ling was occupied by George Lye, a butcher, and the woman was in the habit of going there to do housework. She went there on Friday, and was discovered at the house dead on the following morning. Her head was terribly cut, as if she had been attacked with a cleaver. The place where the murdervfascommittedis an isolated spot nine miles from Yeovil. 'Lye was apprehended on Sunday night at Charton Adam five mileslrom the scene of the murder, and was on Monday brought before the magistrates at Ilminster Police Court and remanded. The inquest on the body of Martha Charles was held on Monday. The evidence showed that the deceased went to the prisoner's house with some clothes she had ironed for him and did not return. She was found next morn- ing at Lye's house brutally murdered, and Lye was miss- ing. The jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against

ALLEGED MURDER IN IRELAND.—The trial was begun at the Wicklow Assizes on Monday of two men, named Hayes and Moriarty, who are accused of being the mur- derers of a farmer named Fitzmaurice in county Kerry. Fitzmaurice was assassinated on the highway when tem- porarily without his police escort—he being boycotted— and his daughter, who was a witness of the crime, was positive in her identification of the prisoners as the mur- derers. At the trial, on Wednesday, evidence was called With a view to showing that the dead man's daughter had given a description of the murderers which did not apply to the prisoners. Being recalled, the girl admit- ted that the description which she gave to Father Shee- han after the murder was not a correct one, and said she knew at the time that it was not correct. The case is not concluded. On Wednesday, in summing up the evidence, Mr. Justice O'Brien said there could be no doubt that the murder was the result of a conspiracy. The jury were about half an hour in consultation, and on their return into court they delivered a verdict of guilty. The prisoners were sentenced to pe hanged within Kerry gaol on Saturday, the 28th April. MR. BALFOUR AT STALYBRIDGE.—On Saturday even- ing Mr. A. J. Balfour addressed a great meeting held at Stalybridge hi connection with the Lancashire and Che- shire Conservative Working Men's Federation. Proceed- ing to discuss the charges made against him by his oppo- nents in his management of Irish affairs, the right hon. gentleman drew a comparison between the a,ction of the present Government and that of Mr. Gladstone between 1880 and 1885. He had not the slightest intention of ex- pending time or patience upon the accnsations made against him by Mr. Wilfrid Blunt, as he promised himself considerable satisfaction in dealing with them on a future occasion more appropriate perhaps to considerations of a personal character. The stories told on Radical plat- forms to bring discredit upon the Government had most respectable godfathers, but he denied that they had the merit of being true. He quoted extracts from speeches and articles of Mr. W. O'Brien in 1882 containing bitter attacks upon Mr Gladstone, Earl Spencer, and the Liberal party, and he especially commended those quotations to Radicals in England and 'Scotland who based an accusa- tibn against the Government upon speeches of men like Mr. O'Brien. Mr. Balfour contended that the Govern- ment were pursuing the same policy as that which corn-, mended itself to the Liberal party four years ago, but that what had changed was the political, interests of the Radical party. DISTURBANCE AT YOUGIIAL. Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., after speaking at Cork on Saturday, went to Youghal on -81112daY, and notwithstanding the fact...that ,the meeting arranged had been proclaimed, the hon. member insisted upon addressing the people. lie made a speech to the Ponsonby tenants at six o'crock in the morning, and in the afternoon proceeded to Green Park with some thou- sands of supporters. But he was stopped by the police when he attempted to speak. The officers attacked the crowd, whom they scattered on Captain Plunkett's or- der. A detachment of the Scottish Rifles also charged the people, a number of whom were wounded.. Mr. O'Brien drove to Canon Keller's house, where he addres- sed a meeting from the terrace. On Monday he left Youghal en route for Dublin. Addressing the people at Killeagh, he said they had won a victory the previous day for freedom of speech in Ireland, which he believed would yet be historic. Fol the first time on record the Government ran away from their own proclamation and were afraid to enforce it. The proclamation referred to in Mr. O'Brien's remarks was one issued by Dt. Ronayne, J.P., Youghal, on the sworn information of Mr. Carey, chairman of the Youghal Town Commissioners. It is stated that interference with the proposed meeting of the Ponsonby tenants might gravely imperil the public peace and promote disorder, and it called on all magistrates and officers entrusted with the preservation of the law to assist Dr. Ronayne in maintaining the peace at the rne,et- ing. TEE LIBERAL LEADERS.—IMPORTANT MEETING. A _ _
,_ljunday,

meeting of Liberal peers and members of Parliament, who held office during Mr. Gladstone's administration, was held at noon on Tuesday, at Spencer House, Se. James's, London.. Mr.. Gkuistone presidedvand amongst those present were Earl Spencer, Lord Herschell, Mr. Childers, Earl Granville, Mr. John Morley, Sir William Harcourt, Earl of Kimberley, Sir George Trevelyan, Mr. Stansfeld, Mr. Mundella, Sir Charles Russel, Lord Oxen- bridge, MT. Osborn Morgan, Sir Lyon Playfair, Sir U. Kay-Shuttleworth, Mr. H. Gladstone, and Mr. H. H. Fowler. Mr. Gladstone, who walked across the park, arrived a couple of minutes after twelve. The confer- ence was private, but it is understood- that the proceedings consisted of a conversational interchange of views on various provisions of the-Local Government Bill. The prevailing opinion appeared to be that the measure in its general character was satis- factory, the principle of direct representation having been adopted as the basis of the new County,Councils. Some objection was taken, however, to the proposal that one-fourth of the numbers of new bodies shall be elected by local authorities, it being felt that to make the Coun- cil entirely representative the whole of the members ought to be elected. Mr. Gladstone, states the Central News, said that the Local Government Bill, which they had met to discuss, was of such a complex character ' that an examination of the whole of its provisions would necessarily occupy considerable time. Hp thought the best course they could adopt would be to hasten the second reading of the bill in the House of Commons, and in Committee to propose such amendments as the state of affairs, and the general views of the Liberal party, seemed to demand. A discussion of a conversational character ensued o and in the result Mr. Gladstone's s.ug- .gestion was heartily and unanimously approved.
