TII E LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. PRINCIPAL CLAUSES. The Local Government (England and Wales) Bill, pre- pared and broughtin by Mr. Ritchie, Mr. William Henry Smith, Mr. Geschen, Mr. Matthews, and Mr. Long, was issued on Monday night The bill is divided into seven parts, the first dealing with County Councils; the second applying the Act to boroughs, the metropolis, and cer- tain special counties; the third dealing with the consti- tution of District Councils; the fourth to boundaries, the fifth to finance; the sixth to supplemental provi- sions; and the seventh to transitory provisions. COUNTY COUNCILS. The opening clauses declare that a Council shall be established in every county, to be entrusted with the management of the administrative and financial busi- ness of the county, and shall consist of a Chairman and Councillors, constituted and elected in the same manner as the Council of a borough divided into wards, with the difference that the Councillors elected by the Counc;! shall be called Selected Councillors instead of Aldermen, and the other Councillors skid' be called Elective Coun- cillors', the latter being elected for three years and retiring together, one for each electoral division. The chairman shall also be elected for three years, and, shall be qualified as a justice of the peace for the county and boroughs within it. AU business done by the Quarter Sessions shall be transferred to the new County Council, Clause 4 provides that "there shall be transferred to the County Council on and after the appointed day the business of the justices of the county out of sessions, (a) in respect of the licensing of houses or places for the public performance of stage plays, and (h) in respect of the execution as the local authority of the Explosives Act, 1875." Clause 7 provides that the Act stisli not affect the power of Quarter Sessions regarding the appointment of chief constables, and that the powers of Quarter Sessions to direct and require constables to perform any duties in addition to their ordinary duties may be exercised both by Quarter Sessions and by the County Council, hut subject to the foregoing.the powers of Quarter Ses- sions with respect to county police shall vest in the Quarter Sessions and County Council conjointly, and be exercised and discharged through the Standing Joint Committee of the Quarter Sessions and County Council. Clause 8 provides that the powers and duties of the Secretary Of State, the Board of Trade, and Local Go- vernment Board, respecting certain enactments, shall, with reservations, be transferred to the County Councils Clause 9 refers to the powers of the County Council as to closing public-houses on special days. They may make, rescind, and vary regulations. providing that all houses and premises in which any intoxicating liquor is sold by retail shall be closed on Sunday, Christmas Day, and Good Friday during the whole day, or during the hours during which by law those premises might other- wise be open and to these regulations the Licensing Acts shall apply after the general annual licensing meeting next after the date of the regulation. Clause 10 provides that "all such powers, duties, and liabilities with respect to the licensing within the mean- ing of this Act of houses and premises for the sale of any intoxicating liquor, or for public billiard tables, as are rested in the Quarter Sessions ef a county, or in any committee thereof, or in the justices of a county out of sessions, shall be transferred to the Council of such county," and that these powers and duties shall be per- formed by the licensing committee of each division of not lsie than six elective councillors, every borough of 50,000 inhabitants or apwards being constituted a sepa- rate licensing division. Clause 11 empowers the Licensing Committee to refuse to renew a license in their discretion, subject to con- firmation by the County Council and to compensation. Clause lg gays :—" The Licensing Committee are re- quired to refuse the renewal of a license for the sale of any intoxicating liquor, upon such repert of disqualifica- tion for holding the license, or such report against the renewal being made as is provided by this section, and any; license renewed in'eontravention of this requirement shall be void." When a person is by law disqualified, either by conviction or otherwise, the justices convict- ing him or voiding the license shall cause a report to be made to the Licensing Committee. Any person desirous that a license should • not be renewed may apply to a petty sessions justice for a report, to that effect, serving notice on the licensee of his intended application within two months before the annual licensing meeting, the notice stating the grounds for the intended applica- tion. The justices shall hear an application for a report in the same manner as if it were an application under the Summary Jurisdiction Acts, and if the justices dis- allow the application the disallowance shall be final. It the justices allow the application and make the report. the holder of the license may appeal to the County Quarter Sessions, which may confirm or reject the report, and a report 80 rejected shall not authorise a Licensing Committee to refuse the renewal of a license. Pending an appeal, the Licensing Committee may sun°- , rise the holder of a license to carry on his business until , the hearing of the appeal. Clause 13 deals )with compensation for the :refusal of a ssnewal of a license. If the refusal of a license under this section is confirmed by the County Council and the, license is applied for by way of the renewal of a license eranted before the passing of this Act, the Council shall nay in respect of the injury caused by the iOBB of the license compensation to such amount. as in default of ~.greement between the County Council and the person claiming it may be determined by an arbitrator, ap- pointed by such Council and person, or in default of their agreeing on snch appointment one appointed by the Chairman of Quarter Sessions of the County. In determihing the amount of compensation regard shall be had in the case of a license to which the Beer Dealers' Retail Licensee (Amendment) Act, 1882, spplies to the discretion of the justices before the passing of this Act to refuse the renewal of the license, hut subject to that consideration, if applicable, the compensation shall be assessed on the basis (if any) between the value of the licensed premises immediately before the passing of this Act, and the value such premises would then have borne if the license had then determined. The compensation shall be paid in the firs, instance out of the county fund, but ultimately shall be charred exclusively to the licensing division in which the licensed premises are situate, but may be charged in other divisions or on the county generally as the Csuuty Council may determine: Clause 15 provides that every road in a county, which for the time being is a main road within the meaning of the Highways and Locomotives (Amendment) Act, 1878, shall be wholly maintained and repaired by the Council of the county in which the road is situate, and the County Council fee dealing with such road shall have the same power and be subject to the same duties es a Highway Board. Clause 16 enables the County Council to enforce the Rivers Pollution Act, and Clause 17 confers on the, County Council the power of making by-laws as the council of a borough have. Clause 24 relates to the Secretary of State's powers respecting the efficiency of the police. If he considers that the police in the county has not been maintained in a state of efficiency in point of numbers and discipline for the year ending 29th seps. tember, he may order the Council of the county to place the .force in a state of efficiency, and the Council of that county shall pay to the Exchequer a sum equivalent to one-half of the pay and clothing of the police of the county for the year. APPLICATION OF THE ACT TO BOROUGHS. • Clause 30 provides that each of the boroughs of Liver- pool, Birmingham, Manchester, Leeds, Sheffield, Bristol, Bradford, Nottingham, Hull, and Newcastle-on-Tyne shall be a county of itself. In the case of Quarter Sessions boroughs having a population of 10,000 and upwards the power of the Council of the boroughs as local authority under any Act shall not be transferred to the County Council, but subject to the provisions of this Act the boroughs shall form part of the county for the purposes of this Act, and the parishes shall be assessed to county contributions. In the case of Quarter Sessions boroughs under a •population of 10,000 Clause 34 provides that "Then: shall be transferred to the County Council the powers, duties, and liabilities of the council and justices, as re- gards asylums for pauper lunatics; also the powers of the Council of the boroughs as regards coroners and the re-appointment of analysis inspectors, and under the Acts relating to reformatory and industrial schools and fish conservancy, and explosives, and under the High- ways and Locomotives (Amendment) Act, 1888." The area of the thorough 61)0 17e ip.cluded in the county, and it anal be in the' Power of the Queen, on petition from , the Council of the borough, to revoke the grant of a Court of Quartet Sessions and the Commission of the. Peace, which will become merged in . the Parliamentary division of the county. Clause 36 provides for the application of the Act to the metropolis 'as the county of London, taking power to Hes Majesty to appoint a sheriff and grant a Commission _ of the peace and Quarter Sessions. to the county. The property, debts, and liabilities shall be apportioned between the portions of the county within and without the metropolis in a manner determined by agreement or srbitration. The powers, duties, and liabilities of the ; Metropolitan Board of Works should be transferred to the London County Councils, and the Board should cease to exist after an appointed day. , DISTRICT COUNCILS IN COUNTIES. . Clauses 41 to 44 deal with the establishment of dig' irict councils in urban and rural districts, councils in ' boroughs, country districts, and the number of council- ors and wards in snc:ll districts. Every county is to be • •fivided into county districts consisting of urban districts and rural districts, every existing urban sanitary dis- trict becoming an urban district tied 'every rural sanitary district a rural district. Where a county district is a borough We council of the borough, consisting of the mayor, aldermen, and councillors shall he the council of the district and shall retain its existing name. Where a county district is not a borough ihe council ef the district shall consist of a chairman and councillors and shall be incoporated by the name of the Council for the district, and elected and constituted like the Council of a borough, with the same designations as the council- lota of the ,County Council, the -chairman not being a justice of the peace. .The District Councils shall have transferred to them the powers, duties, 'of the Improvement Commis- sioners or local hoard if it is an urban district, or of the rural-sanitary authority if it is a rural district, together with certain powers in relation to roads and the liability of justices out of session relating to the licensing of gang masters, the grant. of pawnbrokers' certificates, the

licensing of dealers in game, hawaers' certificates, pas- sage brokers. and ernitrrant runners' certicates, pedlars'' certificates, the ab.lition of and alteration of fairs, Fad the execution of the local authority of the Acts re lag to petroleum, infant life, protection of doe

At 'Armagh. on Tuesday, Miss Prior, daughter of the late Colonel Prior, residing with her mother' was remanded on the I charge of causing the death of a child named Slavin whom she took charge of threfa yeais.ago. ~The child's body was found on Tuesday lying in the kittiteu boiler, and the accused told her sister she had killed te.child. SHoCEING DIeCoVERY AT STOCEPoRT.—On Wednesday .morning the dead body of a little girl, aged four, the child of a Jew living in Owen-street, Stockport, was • found by scavengers while emptying a closet at her father'S house. The child had been missing eight or nine months, and most extensive search had been made for it. The body is in a dreadfully decomposed condition, and has been removed by the Police in a boX to the work- house, where an inquest will be held. It is thought the child has fallen into the closet while playing. div.head: ALLEGED MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT iGRA.PPENHALL. _ . _ •
div.p: ALLEGED MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT iGRA.PPENHALL. _ . _ •

- -- At Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Mr. Edward Greenall and other magistrates, four Irish labourers named Gaffney, Moran, Gibbon, and Callaghan, were brought up on a charge of having, on Saturdayl the 24th instant, feloniously assaulted Police Constable Millington, at Grappenhall, with intent to do him grevious bodily harm. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence.—Superintendent. Hollingworth said that the four prisoner's were charged with feloniously wounding and kicking Millington whilst that officer wit in, the eickation of his duty, at Grappenhall. He would ask the Bench to hear the evidence of the constable, and then they would be able to decide whether to com- mit the prisoners for trial, or deal summarily with the case.—P.C. Millington deposed that at about 10-20 on the night of Saturday last, he was on.duty in Grap- penhall village, when he saw a large number of Irishmen come out of the Barry Arms. Some of them proceeded in the direction of Grappenhall Bridge. He heard a noise and went in the direction whence it came. He saw ttvelve or fourteen Irishmen, amongst them being the four prisoners. Prisoner Gaffney was drunk and appeared to be Causing more trouble than the rest. Witness asked him to go home and he then commenced using abusive language. Witness asked him .his name, and took hold of him, and Gaffney then said, "Now, boys, let's give it him." He then got hold of witness and knocked his knee into his stOniach. Prisoner Callaghan took hold of witness lay the collar, and threatened to 'strangle him. Prisoner Moran then seized witness by the leg and threw him to the ground. The prisoners I after that kicked him about the ribs and about the head. One of them struck him in the forehead with his foot, and all the four prisoners kicked him. Someone was ' heard approaching, when they all ' ran away. Witness was eventually taken home by William' Lomas and another man.—Dr. Willett deposed that onSunday morn- ing he was called to see Constable Millington. He at- tended to his injuries, and found an incised wound on the left side of the head, and a contused wound, on the forghea.d. The constable had also received conifiderable violence on the right side of his body, The wound on .the forehead was a dangerous one.—William Lomas, Grappenhall, stated that on .the night in question he was near Grappenhall Bridge, when he heard cries of "help," and "murder." ' Herniate where the cries proceeded from, and saw a policeman on the ground. Some men were running, away from the place. Witness and another person took Millington home.—This was all the evidence adduced for the prosecution.—Mr. Browne : One tale is good until another is told.—Mr. Greenall : It seems to be a very serious case.—Mr. Browne skid' that the pri- soners had never before been charged with any offence. —ln answer to a question from the Bench, Dr. Willett said that the constable was not yet out of danger.— Superintendent Hollingworth : Then I ask for a remand. It is not right that we should deal with the. prisoners to-day,unless he is out of danger.-Dr.Willett : I anlafraid of erysipelas of the scalp setting in. He was scarcely fit to 'come this morning, and possibly he may become worse. —After a little discussion the prisoners were remanded until the following day, bail being refused. ~ At the Occasional Court House, Warrington, on Wed- nesday, the four prisoners were brought up on remand before Mr. James Marson.—PA). Millington repeated evidence given by him before the magistrates at Dares. bury, and added that after the occurrence he sent infor- mation to Sergeant Booth. Stockton Heath. The ser-' geant came soon afterwards, and they went to a Mrs Meeny's house in search of Gaffney, who lodged there. They them saw eight Men, among whom were the pri= Boners. He identified them, and was then taken in a trap to the house of Dr. Willett. In answer to Mr. Browne witness said that he went inside the Bar'ry-Artn% to order the men out, as it was after ten o'-clock.—Dr. Willett also repeated his evidence.—William Lomas, coal merchant, Grappenhall, having • given evidence, Sergt. Booth•depoied to the apprehension of prisoners.-,-For the defence, Joseph Whittle, carter, Open.shaw, said that he was staying with some friends in Grappenhall. He was in the Berry Arms shortly after ten o'clock on Saturday I night. He went out just after the police officer. About twenty Irishmen went towards Grappenhall Bridge, and seemed to be going peaceably home. The officer followed about three yards behind,. The Irishmen were making no row at all, and there was not the slightest necessity, in his opinion, for the policeman.—Martin Meeney, labourer, Grappenhall, also said that there was no row among the men—Mary Meeney, a widow, mother of the last witness, said that a little after 10 o'clock on Satur- day night sh,e went towards Woodcock's shop, and when she get to the bridge steps she heard a noise on the other side of the canal. She saw a man.standing on the brow of the bridge on the opposite side to where the row seemed to be. She went to him and found it was Antony Callaghan. He was putting tobacco into a new pipe, and he was twenty or thirty yards away from where the row was. She left him standing there and went home.—The magistrates committed prisoner for • triaL—Mr. Browneitsked- that the prisoners should be liberated on bail.—Superintendent Hollingsworth in- timated that he should reqnire substantial sureties.—The Bench said that they wcalld allow the 'prisoners bail in twO sureties of £145 each. • , ,

A JOKE WHICH BROUGHT TEARS TO HIS. EYES. Three commercial travellers sat over their wine and cigars one day after dinner, in a comfortable inn in Devonshire. They were "jolly good fellows," knowing each other as Torn, Dick, and Harry. After comparing notes on the state of trade, etc., jokes and stories went around, till, at last, Tom and Dick began chaffing Harry on the shabby condition of his head, for his hair was fast fallingout, and the sparse quantity he still retained was quite gray, and both de- clared he had deceived them concerning his age, for his scanty gray hairS proved that ha had already "fallen into the sear— the yellow leaf.' Dick declared that he knew of a sure remedy. Harry innocently and anxiously inquired whit it was. Dick told him: "Cut half a dozen red onions into thick slices; rub your head thoroughly with them, and—leaving the slices on your head—sit in the hot sun for three hours 1" "Nonsense 1" harry objected. "Well, if you don't choose to try it, go bald I" Harry secretly resolved to try it, and did. The next day his misckievous friends spied him sitting in the sun, in the stable yard, his head plastered with onions, his eyes full of their juice, and streaming with tears. The shout they set up told Harry that he was sold, and but for Tom's interference Dick's head would have stood in need of a plaster. Dick apologised, and made amends by Informing. Harry of the admirable qualities of Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Rair Re- storer, which never fails to restore the hair to its natural colour, prevents it from falling out, and gives it the luxuri- ance and silken glossiness of youth. TIIESDAY.—Bef ore Messrs. Greenall (in the chair), C. Parr, J. Marson, W. Long, and H. Neild. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—Josepla Mitchell, on the 2nd instant, at Hatton, fined 5s and costs; Matthew Lewis, on the 4th instant, at Little Leigh, fined 2s 6d and costs; John Robinson, at Little Leigh, on the 18th instant, fined 5s and costs.

--- UNLICENSED DOGS.—Joseph Ashbrook, Little Leigh, for keeping a dog without a license, was ordered to pay the costs of the summons, 45 6d.—Henry Taylor and Joseph Leicester were each ordered to pay a fine of 2s Cid and costs for a similar offence. _

SLEEPY DRIVERS.—Thomas Pemberton was fined 5s and costs for having been asleep while in charge of a horse and cart, and John Pilling was fined 2s 6d and costs for a similar offence: , APPLICATION.—An application was made by Mr. Alfred Woods for a renewal of the dramatic license in respect to the Large Room, Grappenhall.—lt was granted. QIJAREELSOME NEIGHBOURS.—WiIIiaIn Bostock was summoned by Sarah Gleave for having used threatening language to her on the 28th of February, and Joseph Gleave, her husband. was stunmoned for having assaulted and threatened William Bostock.—The parties live at Stockton Heathr and are neighbours.—The Bench, after hearing evidence, erdered Bostock, Joseph Gleave, and Sarah Gleave.to be each bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for the next six months.

About noon on Wednesday, over 100 yards length of the railway between Newcastle and Kilcoole, county Wicklow, was washed away by the sea. Traffic wa* suspended fpr several hours. The Prince of Wales left Croxteth Hall on Saturday( and drove, in company with the Earl of Sefton, to Edge' Hill Station, from which he travelled by special train to London. Before quitting Liverpool his Royal Highness cordially bade adieu to the Earl of Sefton and the Mayor clf the city. GLAMORGANSIIIRE (GowEre DrviszoN). ELEcTiox.—The election of a member to fill the vacancy in this division occasioned by the death of Mr. Yeo took place on Tues- day, but the result was not declared until noon on Wednesday, when the numbers were announced as fol- lows : Randall (G.L.) ...... .......... 3,964 Llewellyn (C.) .................. 3,358

The representation remains unchanged, the late mem- ber being a Gladstonian. Mr. Ye° was returned unop- posed at the last election, but in 1885 there was a con- test, Mr. Yeo being returned by 5,560 votes against 2,103 for Mr. Miers (C) ; majority 3,457. "BANQUET TO MR. CRAMBERLAIN.—A public reception was given to Mr. Chamberlain on Wednesday in Bir- mingham in recognition of the success of his mission to Washington. In the afternoon the honorary freedom of the borough was conferred upon him by the Mayor in the presence of the Corporation ; and in acknowledging the honour the right hon. gentleman expressed the pride he felt in being the first honorary freeman of the town. As to the mission itself, he had striven to promote, friendly and neighbourly feeling between Canada and the United States' and though even the final settle- ment should be delayed, he confidently asserted' that much had been done to secure the primary object of re- moving irritation and misunderstanding and to pave the Way to a peaceful and amicable arrangemen.t.of all queS- tions between America and Great Britain. In the even- ing Mr. Chamberlain was entertained at a banquet in the Town Hall. Dr. Dale proposed the toast "Our Guest," and in responding Mr. Chamb&lain said, with regard to the fisheries difficulty, that he found both the United States and Canada anxious to deal with the question in a spirit of equity, and although there were times when their task seemed, almost hopeless, they were encouraged to persevere to the end in the hope of finding some satisfactory compromise and at last they succeeded. The toast " Ottr Kinsmen" was given by Mr. John Blight, who spoke of the scheme of national federation as nothing but a dream, the tariffg that some of the colonies imposed and the foolish foreign policy of successive British Governments being sufficient to prevent its malisation. But he had the greatest pos- sible belief in the future of those colonies and in the con- tinual strengthening of the amicable relations becween. them and this country, sd that ultimately WC thnuld be united by sympathy, communion of interests, and per- petual peace.

in Mr. Goscnme had a'diffic4 task before him the Hoese of Commons;on Monday,in expounding a Budget of unusual clemplexity; and if is due to him to state that he sustained his character as a skilful -manipulator of figures. Perhaps we ought to say that he enhanced his reputation, for it must he remembered that he cut a rather sorry figure Isat year, and was taken severely to task by Lord ItAseoLen Cnrreenru, for the unscrupulous way lfl which he laid his hand on the Sinking Fund. It is pretty easy, of ,course, to pay one's way with revenue rising to a surplus; and, with the im- provement of trade which is signalled, Mr. °Townes, as Chancellor of the Exchequer,- is in the happy. position of having a surplus of i2,16.5,000—the largest surplus since 1873-4, when, -sa most tradesmen remember, everything went "booming along." There was a greater than gosenes at the head' of affairs at that,time ; 'and 'there was a promise, in view of the large surplus Of six millions, of the abolition bf the Income Tax. But the people were stricken, with folly. M. DISRAELI, and not Mr. GLADSTONE, became 1/rime Minister, and to-day the Income Tax site like the Old Man of the Sea upon the shoulders of People. Mr. Goscnis is not Mr. Ginn:from: in 'batters of finance; there is no prosPect of the :abolition of the Income Tax, for the most that the Present Chancellor :of the Exchequer ,can 'see his way to afford is a paltry reduction of one penny the pound. People, to be sure, are glad of that, for their gxpectations are small when there is a Tory Government in office. But why should country continne to carry the huge burden of a war-tax when the nation is at peace? The Income Tan is to be sixpence in the pound for the Current year; it will drain the community of some ten or twelve millions,- although we are neither at War nor have thee prospect of war. Why e hould this be so ?. This is a question which the people should ask themselves, and which should be put -again and again in the House of Commons. The at't is, our legislators have got into extravagant 4bits ; and they have come to deal with and ex- Vaud the Income Tax as if it were to be a permit-- sent source Of revenue. And permanent it will become if the Radicals do not bestir themselves, artd assist such politicians as Lord BaNDOLDN extracsiu. to lay bare and check the wastefulness whin is going on in almost every department of 'the public service. • • It is curious to note that the total increase in the national expenditure is about equivalent to the total at present received from, Income Tax. In 1874, when Mr. GLADSTONE proposed, if he were returned to office, to abolish the Income Tax, the taal expenditure was £74,604,000; but the total exPenditure for the year just ended was £87,424,000—an increase, broadly' speaking, of no lei% than £13,000,000. The Income Tax during the past year has yielded just over £14,000,000; and it comes really to this—that the excess, the 'ever expenditure, is about just as ratich as is de- .rived from this too-convenient impost.. Assuming that Mr. GLADSTONE had been returned to power in 1874, nobody doubts that he would, as pro- Taised, have got rid of the Income Tax; and it is ernatter of course to say that the Tories when they succeeded him, would not have, dared to restore it, except for actual war expenditure. During the last 13 years-'that is to say, from 1874 to last year—the Income Tax has produced on an average, some ten millions a year—or, a total in the 13 years of neaTly £130,000,060. But we have had one or two "little wars " in that Period, and they have cost, say, £30,000,000 at the outside: Income Tax should, of course, be levied for war purposes; and, if the nation had been fairly treated, thirty millions, and not one kindred and thirty millions, would have been • Obtained by was; of taxation for war purposes. Or to put it in another way, if M. GLADSTONE had been permitted' to carry out his plan ' for abolishing the Income Tax, to be revived only 'in came of war being imminent or actual, there would have been a saying to the Oatiun of ONE HUNDRED MILL4ONS of money; and, as the extra money has been spent wastefully and extravagantly, it is not too much to say that the nation has been plundered to the tune the hundred millions during the past 13 years. The remedy for this monstrous state of things is not to be found in reducing the expenditure for the coming year by a miserable half-a-million as GoscHEN proposes ; it is not by reducing the Iticome Tax from sevenpence to sixpenpe that the , SatiOn is to. obtain relief, but by lopping off this, War tax altogether. The nation cannot both eat Its cake and have it: if our legislators are to be Permitted to spend close on ninety millions every so-r when seventy ought to suffice, it is a matter c).,! course to expect that, whatever business is done, there will be less return for the 'capital of the erchant and the tradesmen, and less chance of an itoproved wage for the workman. It is to the QrErlit of Lord HANDoLen CatTecniu that he has 4st his face against the extravagance which has 1!°1:ne under his observation; and we cannot but nark that Liberals .are somewhat neglectful of dray in that they do not pay more attention !o these things. As for Mr. Gosemts, he is simply Itiggling with figures; and he does it cleverly, it uat.be admitted. His scheme of local govern- _4llletlit finance is a robbery of Peter to pay. Paul; t it is a robbery when all is said and done. The .41_411.fact of the Budget is thatin a period of Peace, amid talk of Retrenchment and Reform, we are ing saddled with an expenditure for the forth- , aling year of £86,910,000. It is a great' deal o much. Our vast expenditere saps the ener- gies 1 traders, and capitalists; it robs the worker
habil
of a portion of the fruit of his toil; it is immoral, for it is extravagant—it is a bad example in the ltlghest places of the land. •

THE IRISH SECRETARY has been on the rampage at Stalybridgi. He is not like his uncle the PRIME MmussEß, a master, as Lord BRAcoNs- FIELD styled him, of flouts and gibes Ind jeers; but he is an apt pupil in the alt of saying dis- agreeable things in a disagreeable way. He has te6/1 hard Jilt of late—Mr. W. O'BRIEN has run him through and through—and might be excused for retorting :freely ; but to make retort the staple of his speech is to .confirra•the impression pre- viously made that he is a great man amongst little men, but .a little man amongst s great men. It is suggestive that Mr. BALFOUR could not refer to Mr. GrdinwrinfE without home follower calling out "Shoot him ;" and it is further noteworthy that Mr. BALFOUR had nothing to 'say in the way of reproof to this santuniary potticiaii. The oddity of the whole thing in this connection is that the OME SECRETARY laboured hard and long, and with some degree of success, to prove that the pre- sent Administration were, as to Coercion, following on lines laid down by the previous GLADSTONE Government. But if, in the judgment of Mr. Betrornes supporters, the leader of the Liberal party ought to be shot for the policy he pursued,• it would be interesting to know why Mr. Bei- FOUR should not also be treated to a dose of lead for striving, as he says, to tread in the same path. But Tories do not reason on these matters or they would cease to be Tories; and Mr. BALFOUR evidently knew his audience when he sought to make out that Coercion in his case had been suc- cessful. He knew better than boast in the House of Commons that they had "not failed to vindicate the law of the land f' for that is precisely where the Government have failed. It is the law of the land (in Ireland) that Irish newspapers shall not publish reports of th* proceedings of the National League in districts where the League has been proclaimed. This vile instrument for the torture of the Press was forged with 'a view of suppressing the National League. But has it sucteeded ? Is the law in this respect vindicated? Why, it is notorious that it is openly set at defiance. There is not a Nationalist paper published that does not in this respect break the law every day it' is issued. Mr. %mint has ridicul- ously. "failed to vindicate the law of the land." He has here and there prosecuted an editor, a printer, or a newsagent; but he has not stopped or friglltened thereat; they have simply laughed at him and gone on breaking the law. To such an extent has this proceeded that Mr. BALFOUR in th.eimatter of these press prosecutions has been beaten out of the field. Every, news- agent in Ireland who sells "United Ireland". or wtfie "Nation "breaks the law every week of his life; and yet Mr. BALFOUR is helpless; he has ceased to endeavour to "vindicate the law." The weapon has broken in his hand, yet in his blind impotence he says no responsible statesman has dared to bring it seriously forward in the House of Commons that the liish‘ Secretary has inter- fered with the press. Dared! Dared to encounter this whipper-snapper of a BALFOUR! Thou wear a lion's hide! Doff it for shame And hang a calf-skin on those recreant limbs. The IRISH SECRETARY has been let alone as to press prosecutions, because he has had to let press prosecutions alone. As he is professedly so valiant, let him, if he dare, take action against the editors, printers, and news-agents who are to-day setting him and his Coercion Act at defiance. He will soon see whether the matter will be brought "seriously forward in the Hong of Com- mons. Mr. BALFOUR is a coward on this issue, and lie knows it; and yet he has the "measureless audacity" to talk of de lack of courage of his opponents when they are brought "face to face" in the House of Commons. "Face to face l" Has the IRISH SECRETARY forgot—no, he will never forget—that Mr. WILLIAM O'BRIEN met him "face to face" in the House, and challenged him to make good the insinuation that the member for Oork County had, whilst:in gaol, sought to shelter himself from the hardships of prison life under the plea of illness? And did Mr. BALFOUR accept the challenge? No, he failed to sustain what was found to be a malignant and unfounded assertion; and he stands before the. House of Commons and before the British public as'a convicted and near relative of a "SALISBURY." His speech at Staly- bridge is characteristic ;it is bitter, flippant, and cynical. He knows no remedy for Irish ills but force, and force is no remedy. A nation is not to be mtkle peaceful and prosperous by a (Coercion 4.ct administered with flouts and gibes and jeers.

The postponed Budget resolutions will be considered in Committee of Ways and Means on Monday, April 9. DAIRY SenooLs.—At a meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture on Saturday, the Duke, of Westminster presiding. a paper by Mr. T. Rigby on the report of the Departmental Commission on Agricultural and Dairy Schools gave rise to some discussion. A resolution, moved by Mr. Rigby and seconded by Mr. G. Slater, urging the claims of Cheshire to the establishment of such an institution as appears to be contemplated, was passed. LOCAL LAW CASE: Lever and Co. v. Leaker.—Mr. Justice Chitty, in the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, on Tuesday, gave Mr. John Cutlet, who applied on behalf of the p4.intiffs, the well-known manufacturers of," Sunlight" soap at Warrington and elsewhere in Lancashire, leave to serve notice of motion with the, writ for the first day in next sittings before Mr. Justice Kay, agtfinst the defendants, Messrs. Leaker, who carry on basi- -1 ness at Swansea.

" ORLORO-LINSEED" ()Mel Lozenges, post tres,-7d. Kay Bros.. Ld.. Stockport.—Adot. VENTING SPITE ON A DOG.:-.-At Dareilmy Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Joseph Schofield, a dealer, of. Northwich, was summoned for having, on the 101 h inst., illtreated a dg belonging to Mt. Rutter, of Whitley. The prosecution was conducted by In- spector Aplin, of the R.S.P.C.A.. who said that on the date in-question the defendant went to the house of Mr. Rutter, farmer, Whitley, to try and sell some 'salt. Because none was purchased, he fetched a whip from his cart, and with the butt end of it he cruelly beat a valuable colley dog that yds chained in.the yard. Re did so, apparently, out of spite, because he had not been able to sell any of his salt. For the defence, Schofield alleged that the /log attacked him, and tore his coat, and he lashed at it with the whip to keep, it away from him. The magistrates came to the conclusion that the defendant; was guilty, and imposed a fin e Of 5s and costs, 21s 6d in all, or, in default of pay- ment, a fortnight's imprisonment. "AN OLD RUSTY WEAroN."—The "Manchester Examiner and Time" says :—Qn Monday, wWar- rington tobacconist was lined a shilling and costa , for haying exercised his ordinary calling ' on Sun- day. The proceedings were taken uncler the nearly obsolete Act of 1677, which, like an old, rusty wea- pon, is occaSionally brought outrof its hiding place to fire a chance shot with. Of course, the magili- trates had nO alternative but to convict the defen- dant. The Deputy Town Clerk prosecuted; from which fact it would seem that the prosecution was ordered by the Town Council. But the selection of one in- dividual for punishment under an act which has beconTe practically a dead letter is hardly a pro- ceeding that will commend itself to the average mind. If traders who. exercise their ordinary cal.; tinge on Sunday, " not being a work of necessity or charity." are to be compellbd to shut their shops under the Act; by all means let the thing be done, and be done fairly all round. That will bring mat- ters to a crisis ,; Anti Parliament and the public will be compelled to decide whether or not universal closing shall be the rule. KAY'S Tic Pius, a specific in Neuralgia. • Mr. Burt, M.P., has placed ttrkin the paper a proposal for an address asking tho Queen to ap- point a Royal Commission to inquire as to the amounts paid as royalties, dead rents, and way- leaves on coal, ironstone, and other minerals worked in the United Kingdom, and as to how far these imposts are restrictive of trade and injurious to the public interests. It is high time that an in- , quiry was made into this matter. If a Commission could be got which would do its work properly there would be revelations of a startling character. There is as much money paid for royalty on the coal which carries a liner across the Atlantic as is given to the captain and crew in the shape of wages. This being the case, need we say "There is something awfully wrong ?

WIDNES LORA/ BOARD ELECTION. - Upon certain re- presentations made to him, Mr. Horrabin has withdrawn his nomination, and the expense and trouble of a contest will be avoided. The gentlemen elected are Messrs. D. Brown, D. Wright, F. Heyes, John Taylor', and F. J. Liddell. .

WAYWARDEN FOE WESTON. At the annal meeting of the ratepayers of Weston, Mr. Edward Aaron was re- eleoted Waywarden, an office which that gentleman inas faithfully fulfilled for upwards of twenty years. FREE AVIEDUCH BAZAAR AT WIDNES. The bazaar in connection with the Strday School of Zion Methodist Free Church, was eminently satisfactory. The total amount realised was £lO4, and the debt on the school will therefore be reduced to less than £2OO. A KINDLY ACT.—The other day, Mr. Blackburn, but- cher, Ball-lane, Ditton, put a notice in his wihdow stat- ing that soup would be supplied gratuitously to the poor of the neighbourhood, and we may state that he has had numerous customers, who appreciated his generosity. SERVICE OF SQNG AT WIDNES. The members of the Oakland-strebt Band of Hope on Monday evening gave the service of song "Tempest Tossed" before a large audience in Lacey-strtet schoolroom. Mr. R. Webster presided, and the Rev. J. Bryant read the narrative. The choir was ably conducted by Mr. John Harper, and Mr. R. Briggs was an efficient accompanist. The proceeds will be devoted to reducing the debt on Moss Bank School. _

SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT DITTOS. —On Wednesday night the mangled body of a boy named Jas. Thompson,was found on the line at Ditton Junction Railway Station. The boy who was employed by Mr. David Lewis, grocer, Mersey-road, Widnes, had been to Ditton on an errand, and he was seen on the platform waiting for the train to Widnes. It is supposed that he had attempted to cross the metals instead of walking over the footbridge, and I had been knocked down by a passing train. An inquest will be held to-day. ' Wriaxes SCHOOL BOAUD.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for not sending their children regularly to school :—John Welsh, 9, Sankey- street ; James Hughes, 6, Northreet ; John Bowyer, 50, James-street; Mary Cullen, 53. Dock-street; Denis Malone, 36, Pear-street; William Cunliffe, 83 Travis- street.; John Murphy, 24, Victoria-street; William Gal- lagher, Ellis-street; William Martin, 23, Elizabeth- street ; Peter Connor, 32, Lee-street; Robert Holy, 20, Walmsley-street ; Catherine Gormley, 4, Davies-street; John Grayson, 19, Thorpe-street. The udual fine of 5s was imposed in each case. . A WIDNES STEAMER IN COLLISON.—On Wednesday, the small steamer Widnes, owned by Mr. A. Green, of Liverpool, and manned by • Widnes men, the captain being a man named Moms, came in collision off the Mersey with the steamer Reginald, one of the vessels of the Cork Steamship Company, plying between the Mer- sey and Cork. The' Widnes is engaged carrying lime from Llandulas to Widnes; and she had her sternpost, rudder, and screw carried away, and had to be towed into Beaumaris Bay, where she arrived about ten o'clock in the morning. At the time of the accident a strong wind was blowing from the east, with snow showers and fog, and a rather heavy sed. was running. A BRUTAL WIFE %UTAK AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John Drought, of 3, Gerrard street, was charged _with 'unlawfully; maliciously, and- fitloniously wounding his wife, Elizabeth Drought, with Intent to do her grievous bodily harm. It appears that on Saturday night prisoner asked his wife to send for some beer. 4he told him that as he had given her so little money she had not got any for beer. He then asked her to give him some tea, and whilst she was making the beverage he tried to push her into the fire. He after- wards struck hers violent blow over the left eye and I kicked her severely. Whilst she was down on the ground she felt herself struck with some sharp instru- ment, apd bled profusely. She was treated by Dr. Hutchinson, who signed the certificate produced in court, stating that the woman was unable to attend, as she was suffering from a wound an inch in length over the left eye, penetrating to the bone. Prisoner was, re- manded until the 3rd April. SUDDEN DEATH OF A NAVVY AT Ruscomr.—A power- fully built navvy, named Samuel Davies, supposed to be a native of Devonshire, died suddenly at Runcorn on Sunday night. A week previous he had lived with Geo. Duckett, lodging-house keeper, Church-street, and had then departed to Ellesmere Port to work on the Ship Canal. On Sunday he returned, and a few minutes before teh o'clock. he was walking along the footpath at the cor- ner of Church-street, when a man named Joseph Ban- croft observed him to stagger and fall. Bancroft and P.C. Jackson conveyed the poor fellow to the police sta- tion,.but he was then with dead. The body was after- wards removed to the mortuary. On Tuesday, at the Burial Board Office, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest on the body. Dr. McDougall, who had ex- amined the man, said death was due to natural causes, probably heart disease. The deceased appeared to be about 55 years of age: George Duckett, a juryman, said the deceased was known amongst the navvies as " fight- ing Sammy." He was troubled with his breathing when at his house. The Coroner said there was no sospicion of foul play, and a verdict of natural causes was re- turned.

FRACAS IN A WIDNES PUBLIC-HOUSE.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. H. Gaskell, senr., and Mr. H. W. Deacon, Martin Glynn, a labourer, was charevd, on remand with assaulting ,Daniel Dunn, another labourer. Mr. T. J. Peters appeared for the proseeutor, and Mr. Knowles for the defendant. It ap- peared that Glynn was fined 103 and costs for a similar offence on the previous Thursday, and after leaving the court the men met in Cross's public-house. Glynn asked " which of us is going to pay for drinks ?" Dunn an- swered the question by paving for two glasses of beer, and Glynn having drunk the beverage, knocked Dunn off the stool upon which he was sitting, and gave him a blow on the face that blacked his eyes and stunned him.' —Mr. Knowles, for the defence, pointed out to their worships that the assault was the outcome of drinking, and since the defendant had been in custody he had been attacked with illness, it was supposed with delirium tremens, and he was sent to the Workhemse Hospital. Defendant had promised fo go to the Priest, and under- take to abstain from intoxicating liquor, which had been the cause of his conduct.—Mr. Gaskell said they could not accept excessive drinking as an excuse for a breach of the peace. If he had had delirium trentems he ought to be kept Wider restraint for his own sake. —The defendant was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. MOLESTING A WOMAN AT Wroxis.—Before M. F. I. Gossage and Mr. T. S. Timmis, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Joseph Hargreaves, of 11, Pepper-street, a married man, who is employed on the London and North-Western Railway as a signal man, was charged with committing an indecent assault• upon a young woman named Sarah Ann Quinn.—The prosecutrix stated that she was 18 years of age, and was a domestic servant in the employ of Mr. Thomas Hogan, 15, Ge r- rard-street, Widnes. About 10-15 on Saturday night, the 24th inst., she accompanied Mrs. Gardner, who hves on the Old Marsh, as far as the old stables, and then re- turned along the road with a youth named Stephen Golding. When creasing the London and North-Western Railway near the docks the prisoner came up to them. • Golding and prisoner engaged in conversation, and staved behind. They both then came up and Walked alongside her a little further' and stopped again. The prisoner then came behind her, and putting his arm around her neck pulled her to the ground, and commit-, ted the offence complained of. He placed his knees , on her chest. She screamed, and Golding coming up the prisoner went away. She tad him, however, that she should tell his wife of the occurrence, upon which he used bad language. Quinn further stated that the pri- soner put his fist up at her, saying he would knock her brains out. She then went home in cmhpany with Gold- ing. On the way she met P.C. Evans, and told him what had taken place. By Mr. Lewin: She had never given prisoner any encouragement for his unseemly behaviour. —Mrs. Gardner, wife of George William Gardner, of 3, Old Marsh, Widnes, said after the girl Quinn had left her she had not, proceeded far when she heard her screams. She was too frightened to turn back.—Stephen Golding, labourer,l7 years of age, whose home is on the Old Marsh, stated that he did not see the prisoner knock the girl down, but sat:7 him place his hand on her shoulder. It was dark, and he did not much notice what took place. He did not hear the young woman scream. The only screaming that was ,done was when they were both calling each other nasty names. She called prisoner a scamp, and he called her foul names. Cross-examined by the prisoner: I did not see you dmanything wrong to the girl. I thought you were drunk.—P.C. Evans said the prisoner, when apprehended, stated that he had only put his arms round the girl's neck to kiss her. He now informed the Bench that he knew the girl, because she frequently passed his cabin. She had often struck him on the back and pulled him down to the ground. He had then run after her and served her in a similar man- ner. He was not guilty of this charge.—The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial, but was admitted in bail, himself in £4O, and two sureties of £2O each. 11Ir

The proceeds of the entertainment are to be devoted to wiping off the debt oil the Gymnasium, which object it is to be hoped will be, accomplished. A VIOLENT WOMAN AT WIDNES. —Jane Baker, of no fixed residence, was brought before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. H. Wade Deacon on Wednesday, charged with being drunk and disorclerfr. it appeared that during the night the woman had attempted to strangle herself in the cell, and whilst in the dock she had to be.carefully watched and held by two officers. She screamed and struggled in a most appalling fashion. She was commit- ted to gaol for seven days. A HEARTLESS FATHER Al' WIDNES.—On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Walter Bushell, who had been ap- prehended on a warrant, was charged with haying neglected to maintain his child.—From the evidence of Mr. Treacy. relieving officer, it appeared that on the 26th August, 1888, the prisoner ran away from Widnes, and had left a boy behind him with is one to take charge of him. He had become chargeable to the common fund of tho Present Union.—There were several previous con- victions against the prisoner, and he was sent to gaol for two months' hard labour. THE SUNDAY CLOSING MEETING AT RUNCORN. The Vicar of Runcorn (the Rev'. A. Maitland Wood, M.A:) has received the following letter in reply to the memo- rial which was forwarded from a public meeting _held a short time ago in favour of the Sunday closing of public-houses "Foreign Office, 27th March, 1888. Dear Sir,—l am directed by Lord Salis- bury to acknowledge the receipt of your letter, enclosing 'a memorial passed at a public meeting •of the inhabi- tants, and to say that his lordship will give it his careful consideration.-4 remain yours faithfully, Sichiey Ore- ville. Rev. Maitland Wood. Foarnazt.— Warrington Postal Telegraph Messengers versus Widnes Postal Telegraph Messengers.—This ,match was played at Widnes yesterday. During the first half four minors were scored by the home team. Jugt before the finish of the game, Yates got a free kick for the visitors, and Baldwin being called upon to do the need- ful, kicked a splendid goal. Hamlet, Ellison, Fyrer, and Bennett played a good game in the . forward ranks, whilst Yates and Baldwin played an untiring game at back for Warrington. Rollason was the pick of the Widnes crew. At the call of time for no side, the game, N4tich was pleasantly contested, ended in a win for War- rington by 1 goal to Widnes 1 try and 4 minors. RUNCORN POLICE COURT. —On Wednesday, before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. Hy. Reynolds, Thomas Brown, a young man, was brought up on remand charged with stealing nine pairs of braces from the shop of Mr. Crad- dock, Church-street, under circumstances already repor- ted. The prisoner was sentenced to 14 days hard labour. —James Barge, a' bricksetter, was charged with steal- ing a tin of preserved salmon from the shop of John Dunbabin, Weston Point. The prisoner, on the previous day, went into the shop and pleaded for alms, and his desires not being gratified he snatched a tin of salmon .from the counter and ran off. He was pursued by Mr. Dunbabin, who captured the thief in Runcorn. The pri- soner, who impudently said he thought someone *mild give him some bread to eat to the salmon, was remanded for a week. DRAMATIC Aar AT RUNCORN.—On Wednesday evening the Rev. R. G. Hughes, of Widnes, delivered a lecture on "Dramatic Art" before the members of Brunswick Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society. Mr. Simister, the president, occupied the chair, and there was a capital attendance. Mr. Hughes, in an able manner, traced the origin of the drama, and dealt extensively with English drama. Alluding to theatres, he argned that they were not proper placed to frequent, because the ignoble was mixed with the Noble, and the profound with the ridiculous, and neither the one nor thq other could have tge right effect. He strongly condemned the introduction on the stage of a part o divine worship such as' the offering of prayers, which -as often done in conjunction with some ridiculous scenes. The associa- tions of a theatre were, he said, its worst feature. Dur- ing the evening songs were given by Miss Jones and Miss Birkett, and Messrs. R. Morris and Williams (Weston Point) • and Mr. Hughes gave a recitation. Miss Sinaister presided at the piano. SAVAGE CONDUCT OF A SOLDIER AT WIDNES.—Daniel Gilmour, a diecharged soldier, who took part in the battle of Rorkes drift, was brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Monday. to answer, a charge of felon- iously wounding' Thomas Donovan. It appeared /Oat the men are neighbours hißarn-street, but on Saturday night some difference arose between them. At half an hour past mid-night a man named Thomas Jackson, who liyes in Gerrard-street, saw the prisoner come from his oWri house and go and kick open gm door of Donovan's dwelling, and entered. He draggbd Donovan from the sofa on which he was lying, and kicked him about the head and body in a most ferocious fashion. He then sized a chair, and smashed this piece of furniture oa Donovan's head, which was beaten to a " pulp," and thd injured man bled profusely from many wounds. Shortly afterwards P. Worsfold came upon the scene, and found Donovarrying in a semi-conscious state in a pool of blood. The constable dressed the wounds and sent for a doctor; and then apprehended the prisoner,'who said , he would have hurt Dononn "if he could."—Superin- tendent .7ohnson produced a certificate from Dr. Hutchin- son, who said that inflammation and pleurisy had set in; and the man's life wag in considerable danger. The prisoner was therefore remanded until Monday next. —The condition of Donovan was so criticalon Wednesday that it was deemed advisable to take his depositions. TOWNSHIP MEETING AT WIDNES. The annual meeting of the ratepayers of Widnes was held in the Overseers' Office on Monday after- noon. Mr. James White, the senior overseer,' took the chair, and there were present—Messrs. Fogg, Swale, Pankhurst, Millar, and Goff (assistant over- seer.)—The Chairman, referring to finance; said that last year the Prescot Union demanded £9,730, and the Widnes School Board £3,600, Making a total of £13,330. The rate laid last year was 2s. in the .£, but it did not meet the requirements, and:the balance in hand had' in consequence been reduced from £65785. 2d. to £431 ss. 3d. So that had it not been for the balance the overseers would have been £2OO in arrears. With regard to, last year Mr. Goff, with his usual attention to business, had collected the whole of the accounts, with the exception of two, which amounted to £l4. (Hear, hear.) One account was recoverable, but the other, which should be paid by the Rev. George Bond, vicar of Farnworth, there was some doubt about.— Mr. Swale remarked that the overseers would get their proportion. Mr. Goff : Yes, if he becomes bankrupt, but they had not . made Mr. Bond a bankrupt. The Chairman said considering the number of accounts it was extremely satisfactory that Mr. Goff had collected the accounts with the exception of two.—Mr. Gaff: It is more satisfactory that I have not been obliged to issue a single summons.—The Chairman, referrhig to the coming yea, said he was sorry that the overseers would have to increase the rate to 2s 4d in the £, but it was entirely owing to the demands of the Widnes School Board. Had it not been for the School Board the rate would have been 2s; but, instead of the usual £3,600, they now demanded £4,300, an increase of 000. He did not know why the School Board rate should get up to 84d in the Z.—Mr. Goff kid thp School Board rate had beersinctessing every year.—The Chairman re- marked that the overseers had received from the St. Helens Bank interest amounting to £27 10s 4d on their account. They wished to keep the account at the local bank,but they would not piy theinterest.—Mr, Goff pointed out that the year previous the interest amounted to £6O, but the money had not remained as long in the bank this year.—On the proposition of Mr. Swale, secon- ded by Mr. Millar, the overseers were thanked for their services; arrd it was resolved to submit to the magis- trates the following list of gentlemen qualified to serve as overseers :—Jitines White, J. .Midwood, W. S. Cal- lander, F. Neil, S. Robinson, W. Millar, F. H. Pankhurst, S. Owens, W. Sadler, and A. Parkes.—Mr. Roger Fogg declined to serve another year.—There was no other business of interest. • DUTTON. There have been two rather remarkable disap- pearances from Warrington of late—remarkable because both men were pretty well known. It can- not perhaps be said of them that "They never will be missed,' though the general opinion is that "their room is better than their company. 7. The public will not weep that they are gone, but in one case certain tradesmen are unfortunately " left , lamenting." .

I The en9rotichment upon Gptipls4-3iihsil-laiie is to be inquired into. At the Latchford - Town- L ship meeting, on Mon ay, a resolution was passed instructing the Wa arden to bring the' matter before the Highway d.• Mr. Smith Barry is the owner of land on both sides of the road; but he does not own that which belongs to thy • inhabi- tants; and the inhabitants through their highway authority must protect themselves.

A proriosal, is to be made at the Warrington Town Council, on Tuesday, to: 'prepare an addreps for presentation on the coming of age of Mr. Gilbert Greene,ll. But why should the Town Council take action ? What has this young man done for the ratepayers that their representatives should thus move in the matter ? The age of Chivalry, we know is past. Is it to be succeeded by the age of Snobbery,? It would seem as if the liberal Unionists were about to adopt the policy of war to the knife against Liberals, as recommended by Mr. Cham- berlain some time ago. Mr. John Albert Bright, the eldest son of Mr. John Bright, has accepted an invitation, from the Liberal Unionists, to become a candidate for Rochdale at the next election. This means an attack, of course, upon the sitting member, Mr. T. B. Potter. It is to be hoped that when the tug-of-war cornea John Albert will be badly beaten.

Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., is getting tired of play- ing into the harids Of Irish Tory landlords. Writ- ingto a contemporary, he says :—" Your plan of maintaining the Union is different from mine. The English people feel their responsibility to the loyal minority, but will not tolerate unjust evictions. I have satisfied myself that much of the arrears can- not be Wended on a moral basis." Now, if the rest of the Liberal Unionists will but listen to the "still, small voice" in this way, there will all the sooner be a settlenient of the Irish Question. Gold has been found in Wales, and no there is theft of gold. Two men were arrested at Dolgelly on the charge of stealing ore from the Mount Morgan Gold Mine. The plea of the men is that they abstracted the gold at a date prior to that on which the police were instructed to watch the mine. • .
Gold! gold! gold! sold! .Bright and yellow and hard and cold. Spurned by the young, but hugged by the old To the very verge of the churchyard mould.

Mr. Goscheli's Budget is a thing of shreds and patches and is likely to cause no little confusion. For instance, the repeal of the hawkers' iicensee does not mean what it seems to mean. The haw- ker's license which is to be repealed is a horse tax—a tax of £4 per ,yev for each horse or other' beast of burden, which is payable in half- yearly instalments. Mr. .Goschen shifts the burden by putting the tam on wheels instead of the gipsy hawker. As for the pedlax, he is left' alone, and will be called upon to pay 5s a year as heretofore.

The Welsh are opening the eyes of the Eng- lish. Arrangements are now being made for the introduction of a Bill'intO Parliament con- ferring upon the public right of access to the hills in the Lalo district. In its main features it will be similar to the measure introduced by Mr. Ellis for Wales. A Footpaths and Waste Lana Bill has also been prepared by the Com- mons Preservation Sdciety. Like the Welsh Bill, it will seek to make the County Court the tribunal for the settlement of footpath dis- putes. We are getting a little neaier at last to Socialism and Communism of the right sort.

John Horabin, a milk dealer, of Widnes, seems to have been making too free use of the cow with the iron tail. He was convicted, on ;Thursday, of having supplied milk to which water had been added to the extent of 15 per cent. He disputed the first analysis; but, unfortunately fo'r him, Dr. Campbell Brown's certificate was confirmed by a second analysis at Somerset House. He was fined £lO and costs-t—a severe penalty; but .his 'offence was great. We are glad to see that the Widnes magistrates are alive to the fact that deliberate adulteration is a deliberate fraud upod the public.

Mr. Jolin Croafield, the Liberal candidate for Warrington, yoke with customary frankness, on Monday evening, in-declaring himself in favour of the disestablishment of the Church. That was a good story he told about the Bible Society. One clergyman would not lend the church ' schocil-room for the meeting, because, presumably, Dissenters might attend; whilst another church parson would not attend the meeting, because it was, after all, held in a Wesleyan Chapel. Disestablishment would put ean end to nonsense of this kind; and perhaps rid the church of some of these intolerant clergymen.

That out-and-out Tory journal, "John Bull," is disgusted with the Government for shaping the Local Government Bill to suit the Liberal Unioti- ists. "All this recanting in office," it says, "of the principles upheld while out of office, is fairly sickening, and recalls Lord Beaconsfield's celebra- ted description of a former Conservative Cabinet as an 4 organised hypocrisy.' The 'John Buff ' ex- horks the Tory party throughout the country to do its duty, and to show that it intends to adhere to its own tried principles, whatever may be the makeshifts of a time-serving Ministry." This is ph in speaking; and the sting of it is that it is true.

lie more one hears of the Emperor Frederick I the better he is liked. It is stated that before the beginning of divine service last Sunday, at Charlottenburg, the Elbperor ordered "threw- vent " to be added to the congregational prayer commencing" 0 Lord, pour out thy grace upon the Emperor, our King and Sovereign.' There may not be much in the act itself; but it says much for the manly humility of the man. Let him continue in the path he has marked for him- self, and it shall of a truth be said of him :—" The King's name is +a tower of strength." It seems that the House' of Commons has be- come a place for receiying stolen goods. Nay, ' i start not, reader, we have evidence n support of the statement. Mr. Marriott, Judge Advocata- General, speaking at Barnsley, on Monday, said the Government had been accused of ,stealing the Local Government measure from the Radicals, and it was tau°. The Government cannot, of course, be any better than they should be after this iniquity. But the mischief of i the matter is that, ,after the manner, of otHer snappers-up' of unconsidered trifles, they have so altered some of the articles they have )3tolen as to leave them beyqnd identification.

General Boulanger seems tb be something of a humbug, and the French Government are showing good sense in grappling with him. 'A telegram from Paris says that, at the Council of ministers which assembled on Tuesday morning to deal finally with the charges against General Boulanger, President Carnot, acting op a proposal of General Logerot, signed a decree placing General Boulanger on the retired list. Now, if he would only show himself retiring as well as mtired, there Ivould be an end of him. But that is not the way he has in the army.

div.head: GREAT DISTURBANCE IN WIDNES WORKS.
div.p: GREAT DISTURBANCE IN WIDNES WORKS.

At Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, four rough looking young fello‘k,s named E'dward Ilvnan, of 63, Nelson-street; Michael Noon, 31, Sankey- Street; Michael Keegan, Pittville Cpttages'; and Patrick Killalea, Sankey-street, were placed in the dock to answer several charges of assault. Each prisoner was charged with being drunk and disor- derly. Hynan was charged with assaulting P.S. Clarkson and P.C. Evans; Keegan with assaulting Howard Sacre, sub-manager at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co.; and Killalea Was charged with as- saulting a Pole named Anthony Eavers. The four pri- soners were also charged with assaulting another Pole named Frank Marks. Keegan and Noon were further charged with assaulting Christopher Fox, a prisoner who was placed in the cell with them. From the statements of the witnesses it appeared that about six -o'clock- on Tuesday night the neighbourhood of Messrs. Hutchin- son's works were in a perfect uproar through the conduct of the prisoners. Mr. Sacre, when making his round of the works, found Keegan lying on a black ash ball, and he ordered him to leave the premises. Instead of doing so, the prisoner raised his fist and threatened to throw Mr. Sacre against a revolver, and then a scene of confu- sion commenced. The other prisoners then appeared on the scene, and acted in a very riotous fashion. They ran all over the place, acting with violence towards any person who had the temerity to interfere with them. The two Poles and Mr. Sacre were badly maltreated The police were called in and the prisoners for some time kept them at bay by throwing bricks, clinkers, and other' missies; and work was entirely suspended until they I were captured. At the police station Keegan and Noun were placed in a cell with Fox, who was in custody on a I charge of drunkenness. Immediately the constable had fastened the door the two . ruffians set upon Fox and kicked him brutally. They threatened to serve P.C. Forster in the same manner.—Mr. Smith, .manager of Messrs. Hutchinsons' Chemical works, informed the Bench that the prisoners were not employed there, but were constantly found Inside and causea the greatest trouble and annoyance. On the previous day work was stopped for two or three hours through their conduct.— The Bench fined each prisoner 5s and costs for drunken- ness and disorderly conduct, and for the assaults were sentenced to terms of imprisonment with hard labour as follows: Hynan, ten weeks; Noon, three weeks; and Keegan and Killaler. 7 weeks.

EXTRAORDINARY ADULTERATION OF MILK AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions on ThUrsday, before Mr. H Gaskell, tr. H. Wade Deacon, and Mr. H. Gaskell, jun., John Horabin, grocer and milk dealer, Albert-road, appeared to an adjourned summons .charging him with having, on the 7th February, sold adulterate& milk. Mr, J. 0.. Swift prosecuted on behalf a 16 police authtrities. and Mr. Knowles defended. Mr. Swift stated that on the 7th ultimo Superintendent Johnstone, in consequence of com- plaihts he had riceived, visited the defendant's shop and purchased from Mrs. Horabin a pint of new milk, for which he paid lid. The milk was divided into •three 'parts in the usual way, the de- fendant retaining one sample, Superintendent John- stone another, and the third was forwarded to the public analyst, Dr. Campbell Brown. Dr. Brown certified that the sample contained fat 2.94 per cent., other solid.s 7.29, an that "upwards of 15 parts of added water have been added to every hundred parts of milk." At the first hearing a month ago Mr. Knowles put in a cer- tificate from Mr. Edward Davies, of Liverpool, who stated that the sample sent him contained solids not fat 9.19, fat. 5.03, ash .74 He added that "this sample of milk is not only pure-, but of remarkable richness." Owing to These con- flicting certificates it was decided to send the third sam- ple in the possession of Supt. Johnston to Somerset House; and j. Bell, IT.S.C., •, and R. Bannister, F.C.S. sent a certificate that the milk contained non fatty solids 681; fat 2.79; water 90.40, and added "From a consideration of this result and making an addition for natural loss-arising from decomposition of the milk through _keeping, we are of opinion, that the milk contains not less than 15 per cent of added water. Mn Swifb pointed out that the seal on the bottle left in the possession of Mr. flbrabin, had been broken off and then attempted to bere-affixed hr means of sealing wax, and he alleged that the ianaple of milk had been changed with the wicked and corrupt intention of deceiving the Bench.—Mr•. Knowles stated that the wail was perfect when the bottle was handed to Mr. Davies,. as that gentleman's description of the seal would testily,. but on being returned to Mr. Horrabin the seal was off. The son attempted to affix- the seal with sealing-wax. He continued that his client had acted in an honest and straightforward manner throughout, and a month ago he expressed his willingness to 'abide by the Somerset House certificate. The manner in which the prosecution had acted that morning savoured strongly of persecution. The Bench inflicted a fine of £lO and coAs, £2 45., in- cluding advocate's fee.

GOOD FRIDAY AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES. The anniversary of this great religious event was celebrated in the customary manner in Runcorn and Widnes. To stop the numerous operations that are carried on in a chemical works would entail a I most heavy loss upon the proprietors, but with the exception 9f the men necessary to keep them in proper action the workmen had a holiday. In a number of the manufactories the holidays will extend to Tuesday morning, in others to Monday morning, whilst in a few the men will have to don their everyday clothes this (Sat- urday) morning. At the churches of the Establishment, aad at the Catholic Chapels services ;were held in the • morning and were fairly well attended. The chief aim of the population on a holiday is however to obtain some ,new, pleasure and enjoyment, but on the present anni- versary the atmospheric elements spoiled the nost well laid plans. Throughout the greater portion of the day dark clouds obscured the sky and a drizzling rain fell with provoking persistency. After a train from Liverpool to the Welsh watering places had passed through, Runcorn Railway Station was closed as on Sundays. • Very few passengers left Runcorn by this train. Notwithstanding the bad weather, many persons walked and drove to Frodsham and Helsbv, but the number was far below the avera*. From Widnes Lon- don and North-Western Station excursions were run to Buxton and Blackpool, but not more than 80 passengers were booked., The ordinary trains, however, were well filled with persons departing to the surrounding places to visit friends and acquaintances. On the Cheshire Lines an excursion was advertised to run to Cleethorpes and Grimsby, but in consequence of the prevalence of small-pox at the latter port, the excursion was aban- doned. Numerous passengers, however, booked to Southport by this line. The promenade at Widnes, which has been recently improved at a cost of several hundred pounds. 'presented a lively scene. On the sands was a low,' line of swing boats, which were well pat- ronised by the smaller fry of the epulation, and an en- terprising owner of horses had no lack of customers at a penny a ride. Gingerbread and nuts were dis- played in profusibn on stalls erected along the street. The tide in the river was an excep- tionally high one, and hundreds of persons 'flaked the promenade to view the "waste of water." In the afternoon some hundreds found amusement in watching a football match between Widnes and Holbeck. The visitors had much the best of the play, and the ball was seldom out of the Widnes quarters, but up to within five minutes of time Holbeck had only succeeded in scoring two minor points. Then Parkinson " mulled " the ball in shocking fashion, and Holbeck scored a try, from which a goal was scored. Moved by this reverse, Widnes played with kreater dash, and after some pretty passing by Farrell, Parkinson, and Plumpton, resulted in the latter player planting the ball over the line. The kick at goal failed, and the game ended—Holbeck 1 • goal, 2 minors, to Widnes 1 try. In the evening the Primitive Methodists and the Welsh Wesleyans held tea parties at their respective schools: follo*ed by musical entertainments.

As the most important township in the Union, Runcorn is entitled to five repsesentatives, and eight gentlemen have been nominated. Mr. Thomas 'Kirkham has already signified his refusal to serve, and there ate now left two new candidates in the field in the persons of Mr. Smith and Mr. Jones. Mr. Smith has intimated his willingness to withdraw if Mr. Jones will do likewise, and thus avoia the expense of an election by returning unopposed the five retiring Guardians. Mr. Jones is determined, however, to give the ratepayers an opportunity of expressing their opinions, and it is highly probable that a contest will take place. In that case Mr. H. Linaker, who is the returning officer, will cause voting papers to be distributed on the 7th April, and collected on the 9th. As regards Frodsham Mr. C. E. Linaker has withdrawn, and there are now three can- didates for two seats. It is understood that a contestois certain. In the other places a compromise may be decided tipon. Since the above lines were Tvritten Mr. W. Fisher has withdrawn his nomination, and there is a likelihood that a further withdrawal will take place.

Prove all things" seems to.betheguiding Maxim of the people of this age. This -would be all right, were it not for the "know-ails" in every commu- nity, wtto are sure that every introducer of a new ,idea is a crank," and that every new invention is " utterly impracticable." The astonishing fact is that in this class educated men and scientists are found. In the days of George Stephen- son, the perfector of the locomotiye engine, the scientists proved conclusiveN that a railway train could never be driven by steam power successiuny Withteit peril; but the rushing express trains all over the world show how mistaken they were. Professor Morse was ridiculed when he asserted that he wonld make the lOtning of heaven his,errand-boy, and he was told by scientific men that such a thing was impossible. Yet the news of the wide, wide world, as it is given us each .morning and evening by the electric telegraph, has Made all nations. witnesses. Rev. Now, suppose ten other men should come up and say, We don't believe that there is anything in . that medicine:' 'Well,' I say, have you tried it g' 'No, I never tried it; but I don't beheve there is anything in it.' Of course von discredit their testimony. The sceptic may come and say, There is no power in your religion.' 'Have you ever tried it?' Norno.' Then ayaunt ! " Let me take the testimony of the millions of souls that have been converted to God, and comforted in trial, and solaced in the same hour. We will take their testimony aa. they cry, We are Wit- nesses !' " The proprietors of Warner's SAFE Cure have received over ten thousand voluntary testimonials to the efficacy of that medicine. They have come from almost every civilised country, and they may fairly clain "it has made all nations witnesses.'" The evidence comes from all classes. The highest medical authorities, like Dr. Gustax Weber, of Germany,and Richard H. Gunn, M.D., of New York, and eminent scientists like Dr. Andrew S. Wilson and Dr. George Hand-Smith, of London, are among the published witnesses. Hundred of these testi- monials have been and are being published. They can be easily verified. A standing offer of £l,OOO for proof that any one of them is not true, so far as the proprie- tors know, is a fair guarantee of their genuineness. If a man is suffering from any one of the ailments, of which there are so many, growing out of kidney derangement, is it not foolish for him to refuse to try Warner's SAFE Cure when thousands testify they have been cured byits ? Think of it! The men who refuse to believe that any- thing can be valuable because it is in conflict with old ideas, are the men who *.f get left "_in this world, and go before their time to try another.
