div.head: RUGBY RULES. WEST LANCASHIRE CHALLENGE CUP COMPETITION. FINAL TIE AT WARRLNGTON.
div.p: RUGBY RULES. WEST LANCASHIRE CHALLENGE CUP COMPETITION. FINAL TIE AT WARRLNGTON.

Nothing was wanting on Saturday to make the final contest for the West Lancashire Challenge Cup a grand success. The scene of operations—the ground of the Warrington Club—was in the best of condition, the weather was all that could be wished for, the spectators were present in groat numbers and were full of en-

thusiasm, and last but not least, the merits of the two competing teams Tyldesley and Widnes—were so nicely balanced that not till the whistle of the referee blew "no side" could anyone be fully assured. that the fortunes of the day had been decided. The time ap- pointed for the beginning of the fray was half-past three, but for more than an hour before that time an, eager and expectant mass of humanity—as might be expected al- most wholly of the sterner sex—was pouring across the bridge and along Wilderspool Causeway. Many thousands of spectators accompanied each of the teams,

while Warrington contributed a very numerous con- tingent. The result was that by the time the rival teams put in an appearance the large square arena was completely encircled by a deep band of spectators, the long grand stand was packed with occupants and 'many extemporised platforms in the shape of waggons were equally well filled, while every point of vantage, con- venient or inconvenient, was utilised to obtain the coveted view. Tyldesley were the first to emerge from the Pavilion and they were encouraged by a great shout from their admirers, Widnes, who followed within a few seconds, receiving a somewhat similar greeting. And it may here be noted that there was little or nothing throughout the game which could be construed into an exhibition of the bitter resentful feeling which was supposed by some people to agitate the breasts of War- rington spectators against Widnes players. Excitement and noise there certainly was in plenty, but it was hard to say whether the cheers and encouraging cries were loudest when Tyldesley or their opponents had, or were supposed to have, some advantage, or at all events if the Coals," as they were quickly dubbed, had something the best of it in this respect this was mainly due to the greater elation of their sftpporters. A critical examina- tion of the two teams as they defiled into the field showed that in physique they were fairly well balanced, though Widnes undoubtedly had some advantage in weight and height. On the other hand amongst the Tyldesley champions there were two or three—and notably Berry—who, though not tall, were clearly en- dowed with more than an ordinary proportion of thew and sinew, their strength being of the Hal O'th Wynd type—more substantial than elegant. No delay took place in the settlement of preliminaries, and the players quickly ranged themselves on different sides of the cen- tre line, Tyldesley kicking off with the sun shining pretty brightly in their faces. The opening incidents were all in favour of Tyldesley for the ball was carried into Wiet- nes quarters, and by combined movement on the part of the aigressive team was in less than five minutes from the start carried over the line and a try gained by Hodgkinson. From this Shaw neatly kicked a goal, so that Tyldesley were already in the fortunate position of being eight points to the good. Upon a re-start being made it was seen that the " Chemicals " had in no' way been dispirited by the speedy reverse they had sustained. They continued to play with keen determination, notwithstanding which, *however, they were still kept pretty consistently in their own territory by the dash and combination of their opponents. The display of the previous veek had proved that the Tyldesley forwards had a power about them that was difficult to withstand, but on that occasion the backs showed a considerable amount of weakness. In the final, however, one and all,—backs and fotwards,—of the Tyldesley men reached high water mark and played with a steadiness that Widnes found it impossible to overcome. Berry, who hag' beerf initiated into the mysteries of the game in the Kendil Hornets school, has evidently familiarised his new coadjutors with some of the points—especially rapid and accurate pass- ing—for which the. Westmoreland men are famous. Another good feature in the Tyldesley back play was the continual punting forward of the ball. On Saturday it was a very fare thing for a Tyldesley three-quarter who had possession of the leather not to get a kick in before his opponents were down upon him like an avalanche; and those who have seen the play of good Yorkshire clubs, such as Wakefield Trinity, know that this is a very effective sort of tactics. Widnes, it was generally admitted, played with all their old determination and energy, but they seemed to trust too exclusively to these qualities to be formidable to & pally strong and well- organised team. A little more intelli,gence in the manipu- lation of the ball and a little more of systematic playing into each other's hands would put the chemical toWn contingent into the first rank of Lancashireßugby clubs. The first half of the game was brought to a close without any further score than that recorded above, Nad con- sequently Tyldesley was still leading by eight points to nil. There is little that can be said about the second half. The ball was sometimes at one end of the field and then at the other' though upon the whole the balance was decidedly in favour of Tyldesley. Each side in turn scored a minor, and Tyldesley put in what many people thought a valid claim for a try, but this, after some con- sideration,was not allowed, and eventually a keenly con- tested game ended in favour of Tyldesley by one goal and one minor to once/ninon The following is a list of the two teams, viz :—Widnes: S. Bingham, back; F. Plumpton, Parkinson, and T. Wilkinson, three-quarter backs; R. Barker and E. Farrell, half backs; J. H. Smith (captain), W. Kiddie, D. Harding J. Hardman, J. Bingham, G. Woods, W. Barber, T. Harding, and X. Pennington, forwards. Tylliesley : H. Pearson, back; J. Fearnley, F. Shaw (captain), and W. H. Ramsden, three-quarter backs; Berry and C. Hardman, half backs; G. Woodward, Smith, J. Hampson, T. Hilton, W. Sutcliffe, Ramble, W. Healey, P. Eckersley, and J. Hodgkinson, forwards. Umpires: Messrs.. Trevor Smith and Vickers. Referee : Mr. E. Beswick, Swinton.

div.head: PRESENTATION OF THE. CUP.
div.p: PRESENTATION OF THE. CUP.

As soon asthe game was over a rush of spectators was made to the grand stand, in front of which the trophy hadobeen displayed, and on which were his Worship the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Sutton), Councillor William rierpnint (president of the Warrington Football Club), Air. F. T. Parry (hon. sec. of the West Lancashire Union), and Mr. F. Shaw (captain), and other members of the victorious team., Three cheers having been given for the winners, and for Berry, who had played so well during the match, Mi. PARRY said that as hon. secretary of the West Lancashire Union, he had very great pleasure in calling upon the Mayor of Warrington to present the eup to the I Tyldesley team. The Mesoa, who was received with cheers, said: It

Cheers having been given for the Tyldesley and Wid- nes clubs and for the Mayor, the proceedings were brought to a conclusion. THE FOOTBALL PRESS ON THE CONTEST. The "Football Times" says :—This match was the crowning success of the West Lancashire Union, and all the officials ought to be highly pleased with the grand success. We never remember such a 'crowd and enthu- siasm displayed in a club match in Lancashire or Cheshire before, and we are pleased to inform our readers that considerably over £2OO was taken at the gate. The Executive were congratulating themselves at the Roebuck Hotel after the match. The health of both Tyldesley and Widnes were heartily drunk, and a highly complimentary vote of thanks was passed to the Warrington Executive for the excellent manner in which all the arrangements were carried out. "Philistine," in the "Athletic News," says :—They came, they saw, they conquered. Julius Ciesar's trite expression of his prowess needs only altering to the plural sense to briefly describe the Tyldesley idea of the great match at Warrington last Saturday. Whether this opinion is shared by many at Widnes is not at present ascertainable, but that the game was won within three minutes after the start is an indisputable fact, and thou- sands of spectators were unanimous in declaring that throughout the match Widnes never had a decent look in, but were overplayed and out-manceuvered by a team of smart and " skilful footballers'. How much of their success the Tyldesley men owe to Berry was self-evident to every interested spectator, and there could be no qu4- tion as to the superiority of the ex-Kendal Hornet's dis- play in contrast with any player on the field. He was the captain without the title, and his excellent headwork was fully equalled by his magnificent tactics; not that the other Tyldesley men lagged or were deficient in skill by any means, but the example of the north-countryman infused such an emulative spirit that a weal' spot could not be found in the whole fifteen. Individually they were excellent; collectively they were itnpregnable. Turning to theii. opponents, one could not fail to notice 'the great difference in style and lack of finish and combi- nation in comparison. There was a constant 'failure to grasp the little point of advantage in the hope of secur- ing something better, with the usual sequence--a loss of both. There was no mistaking the earnestness of the players on both sides, a fact which later on in the game claimed the special attention of the referee, but, consider- ing the great excitement under which every player laboured, there was nothing to note in this direction that would not °Apr in any club game. The tackling was certainly robust and very effective. It was, no doubt, meant to be so, and one cannot blame a man wken he puts his hand to something, he does that some- thing with all his might: If nothing else, it secured the vdbiferous approval of a numerous section of interested people who did not stint tioeir pleasing expres- sions of cheering encouragement throughout the game. The Warrington ground was not the one originally se- lected for the final struggle, the St, Helens Recreation be- ing the favoured spot, but owing to a certain young gentleman's mistaken idea that polo is a popular rival of football, the Rec's was declared to be unavailable. It was, perhaps, just as well that it was so, and that the Warrington enclosure was decided on, for the committee may be congratulated that their selection was a wise one from considerations of a pecuniary character, and also as offering aground which is, without doubt, the i most favourable n Lancashire, toth from a player's and spectator's point of view. This decision of change of venue was not altogether to the fastidious taste of the Widnes people, consequent on the enormous amount of love which is wasted among the affectionate dwellers of these enterprising and salubrious villages, and there was a funny rumour going about with its overcoat on that Widnes would decline to play on their neighbour's ground. Better counsels, however, prevailed, though it may be mentioned to Tyldesley's everlasting credit that they were willing to go anywhere to suit the Widnes folk.

With regard to the unallowed claim for a try by Tyl- desley the "Athletic Journal" remarks—" A curious point Is to be laid before the Rugby Union by Mr. E. Beswick, the referee in the West Lancashire Cup final tie. One of the Tyldesley men dribbled the ball over the Widnes lines and was just oil/the point of scoring when he was held on the ground by the Widnes full back. There the pair lay, Fernley making frantic struggles to get at the ball, but the Widnes man would not let him, and one of the defending side rushed up and kicked the ball dead. The referee had no power to give a try in, as the only penalty is a free kick, and this is useless over the lin'es. So the question is going up to the Rugby Union." '

The final struggle for the holding of the English trophy took place at Keilhington Oval, on Saturday, under somewhat remarkable circumstances, and so great was the interest in the event that large numbers of enthusi- asts made the journey from the north and midland dis- tricts, the special service of the railway companies being largely taken advantage of, especially by the residents of the towns more particularly concerned, so that when play commenced there were close upon 20,000 persons present. Ross won the toss, and Bayliss kicked off ex- act-Vat 'the stipulated time. I by two to one. am sure that after the splendid exposition of football which was given last Saturday, all the spectators were anxious for Tyldesley to win to-day. (Cheers.) We have not seen from the Tyldesley club one single bit of unfair play. (Hear, hear.) Football is one of those noble games which, if played in a manly spirit, must do good to the rising generation. (Cheers.) We don't want men to lame each other. but so to play that the best men shall win; and I believe it Is the opinion of even the opponents of Tyldesley that the best club has won to-day. (Cheers.) I am, however, obliged to tell you that if the Warrington team had been playing they would have won the match. (Laughter.) You have all been' delighted with the splendid manner in which Berry played. (Cheers.) Councillor ITILLLitt PIERPODiT : YOU have had speak- ing to you tha chief magistrate of the borough. You ha.4o also had speaking to you a very old and ardent foot- baller, in the person of our friend the ex-president, Mr. Francomb, M.P.—I mean J.P. (Loud laughter.) You need not laught at what is, apparently, a joke, because that may sometime, in all seriousness, become a fact. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. Francomb has said that if the Warrington Club had entered into the competition, in all probability they would have been the winners. lam not going to say that for a moment. As president of the club, I might be excused making such a remark; but, at the same time, am bound to admit that in the play we have witnessed to-day between Tyldesley and Widnes you have had a remarkably fine exposition of the game of football as it ought to be played. (Cheers.) I claim that they are two of the finest clubs yon have in South-West Lancashire, and I claim for my club also that it is equal to the two. I should like to tell you this, gentlemen, that the Warrington Club think so highly of the Tyldes- ley team that they are giving them fixtures for next year. (Cheers.) lam very glad to see that our friends from Tyldesley and our friends from Warrington appre- ciate that fact. I should also like to tell you that next Saturday we shall have a splendid match here, we are playing Dewsbur3r. If 3-ou attend you will see the Yorkshire style of football, and you will be able to make your own comments and form your own con- clusions as to whether our style is better than theirs. (Cheers.) Mr. SHAW (captain of the Tyldesley team) : I feel very thankful this afternoon that the Mayor has handed to us this cup. lam sure he has said everything he could in our favour, and I hope that Warrington rid Runcorn, and some of the other good South Lancashire clubs, will join this contest in future. I think it would kindle the interest which is already felt. (Hear, hear.) I hope our club will continue to play in the same good form during the season.
Warrington were not ble to raise a team on Saturday to meet the Free Wanderers, and consequently the match was postponed. We understand that a fixture for some week night will be made instead.

AT EASTHAM.

We went down to Eastham to hunt up the Ship Canal, and carne back more than half inclined to write a pas- toral. Eastham is not a convenient place to reach when the ferry boats are not running. ' You may get to Lon- don from Manchester with far less trouble and almost as quickly. Probably nobody will be surprised at hearing that the Eastham canal works ait not at Eastham, that they are not even within sight of the village, that they are in fact about a mile away. In our confiding simpli- eity we had expected to find the equanimity of the little ' place altogether upset, its streets swarming with navvies and steam devils, and lots of things; but it was just as quiet and sleepy as ever, and there does not seem to be any likelihood of the prettiness of the thatched cottages and moss-grown red sandstone walls being disturbed at present. We pass through it and along the road towards the ferry for about three-quarters of a mile, when at a turn in the road we catch sight of the broad estuary, on the edge of which are evident signs of something being done. In the distance it looks like a namiw slip of rail- way in course of construction. There are rows of boar- ded sheds, long lines of trucks, and little locomotives running to and fro. Our road is upon high ground, and between us and the works is a great grassy hollow with clumps of trees here and there. We descend, and find in the bottom a temporary railway being made, which upon inquiry proves to be solely for tipping purposes. As we get nearer we find there is a much greater breadth of land on the estuary bank being operated upon than at first sight appeared; the scene becomes very, 'animated, altogetheri novel, and in its way decidely pic- turesque. It s evident that a big work is going on. The vicinity of the central offices and clusters and rows of houses, all built of boards, and everything with a bran- new appearance. The houses are, of course, for the peo- ple employed on the works, and look very neat, with clean bright blinds, and lace curtains to' the windows. There are long lines of clothes hanging out to dry, and women and children here and there seeming quite set- tled and at home, Quantities of newly-felled timber are ' -lying about, helping the illusion; and among the dead branches of a tree lying upon the ground dose to the engineer's office a pretty pye-fineh is. singing his little song most cheerily. When all is finished, there will be great docks here, and tidal locks at the mouth of the canal which will be open at high tides; but, of course, we can see nothing of these as yet. The whole place is in an apparent chaos, filled with life and activity; but the eventful forms into which things will settle can at present only be perceived by the engineers themselves. We start round upon Qur tour of inspection, having first received a warning to take care of our precious selves and ndt get run over by a stray locomotive—a warning we soon find to be not without reason. How in the world were such great enterprises as this got through with before the introduction of steam and railways? I It seems impossible to stir in any direction here without them, and the lines are running about in a perfect net- work everywhere; engines puffing and screeching at you from all parts until it requires an effort to keep your wits about you, and prevent yourself being cut into mincemeat. There are about eight miles of rail laid upon ' this section, three of which run up the side of the estu- ary as far as Ellesmere Port, where docks will be con- structed by-and-bye. There are great engine-sheds, and , smiths' and machine sheds, where all sorts of things' are r being made*: whilst all around is a seeming confusion • of stock and plant, and divers machines, and steam s cranes, and trunks of trees and piles of sleepers. , Some of the men are engaged in making new trucks. ; From the head of the cutting as so far reached, we are within sight of the projecting point known as Pool Hall . Rocks, through which the caisa/ will shortly pass; and . then comes Ellesmere Port. . _

• Rows of workmen's cottages are scattered about here as at the lower end, and everywhere washing seems to be going on, They must be cleanly, folk, these people. The backwoods' likeness is more strongly emphasized here that at any other end, there bejpg patches of clear- ing wherein numerous really large trees have been sawn off and taken clean away, whilst the stumps still remain in the ground, just as you see them in pictures. Upon the Eastham section from six hundred to seven hundred men are employed, who have a mission hall, and we understand, a regularly-appointed missionary.— Manchester City News. INJUNCTION AGAINST THE CONTRACTOR.

In the Chancery Divisioh of the High Court of Justice, London, on Saturday, Mr. Justice Kekewich again had before him the matter of Park Yates v. Walker.—Mr. Farwell applied for an injunction to restrain the defen- dant, the contractor for the construction of the Manches- ter Ship Canal,frpm trespassing onany land the property, of the plaintiff, situated at Ice. Mr. Justice Kekewich, in reply, said in disposing of the motion he should care- fully guard himself against deciding any point which he was not bound to decide on the motion. With regard to the roads there was a bona fide dispute as to their being public or private, and this question would require care- ful investigation. All he decided now was that on this part of the case there was foundation for the plaintiff's claim to be entitled to some compensation. On the other part of the case his Lordship said the plaintiff gave the Manchester Ship Canal Company notice of his rights. Two courses were then open to the company—either they could disregard his claim and run the risk of an injunc- tion, or serve him with notice under the statute and pay sufficient security into court. The company took the first course, and the plaintiff was entitled to say that he would not consent to be turned out of possession except on proper security being given. It was very well to say that Mr. Walker was perfectly solvent, and that the plaintiff would be compensated at the proper time, but the plaintiff was entitled to say, as he did, that he wished to have the money secured according to the statute. On the question of injury, his Lordship said it was argued on behalf of the defendant that the injury was not Irre- vocable, put the question was whether there had not I been " permanent " injury in respect of which a reversioner could alone claim. It was said that the hedge had been restored and new stone posts substituted, but the removal of a hedge and the taking stone posts from the soil did constitute permanent injury in the sense that it would be permanent if not repaired. Then, on the question of the balance of convenience and incon- venience, his Lordship said the balance was in favoiii• of restricting the Manchester Ship Canal Company, like other bodies performing great public works, within their statutory rights. The difficulty would be at once removed by the company serving the plaintiff with a proper notice. There would, therefore, be an injunetion against the defendant in the terms of the notice of mo- tion. Mr. Hassell having givenoan undertaking 'satisfy- ing the plaintiff, nothing need be said with regard to him. —Order accordingly. • VAGRANTS AND THE CANAL. The " Liverpool Weekly Mercury" says :—The rate- Payers of Manchester have just had an intimation that the cutting of the proposed Ship Canal has some serious drawbacks. It was reported on Thursday to the Board of Guardians that a swarm of casuals have to be accom- modated night after night at the workhouse. During: last week there were 274 admitted, as compared with I /40 in the corresponding montlf of 1887. It is the opinion of Mr. George Rooke, who presided, that this increase is likely to be permanent; but obviously there is no danger of that. Thn Master was better informed .of the cause of this access of vagrancy, which compels the officials to make all kinds of shifts for the reception and lodgment of the applicants. The intelligence has travelled far and wide that men are wanted for work connected with the Ship Canal, and the adventurous are flocking in crowds to the spot. Of course they earshot be all employed, no matter how vast the undertaking; but they come all the same just as the superfluous agri- cultural labourers prdinardy drift to London Liverpool, and other populous places even when the labour market is already full. During the winter season there is always a great deal of labour partially or wholly idle. The pressure lifts, with the spring, awl does not descend again until the close of the harvest and the return of cold weather. But at any period of the year there would be a: rush to such an undertaking as the Ship Canal, which needs an immense amount of unskilled service, and pays reasonably good and certain wages for a con- siderable period. The construction of a line of railway produces a similar state of things, so that we heed not assume any exceptional lack of general employment , from the growth of vagrancy in Manchester. So long as the works of the Ship Canal are in progresa they will fur- nish an attraction to the unemployed, and hundreds'or thousands will have their tramp in vain. It is none the less likely,that the unskilled labouring class are finding the means of living harder to obtain. Great enterprises are not now so frequent as during the years of rapid material development, and the decrease of land cultiva- tion is adding to the ranks already overcrowded, with results which are felt everywhere, but only become vivid when a centre of attraction is cfeated which draws the idle together from a wide circumference.

MOVEABLE DWELLINGS AND LOCAL , AUTHORITIES. 'At • Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, John Richards, a ganger on the Moore section of the Ship Canal works, was summoned for Raving, on the 27th of February, at Moore, occupied a dwelling-house without having obtained permission to-do so from the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority. He pleaded guilty, but said that he did not know that he was doing anything wrong. —Mr. Farrington, inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sam-

tary Authority, said that the defendant had erected the dwelling for himself, and for workmen engaged in con- nection with the Ship Canal. He had occupied it with- out having a: certificate of occupation, but had \ ilone so in ignorance of the law. There was no wish4o press the case.—Defendant : It is a movable place.—Mr. E. preenall : Still you are living in it P—Defendant : Yes. —Mr. W. Long: Do you take lodgers ?—Defendant: Yes. sir. It all consists of timber. I do not know the rules of this part of the country. I never wanted it (a certificate) before. All round the Midlands we never had to have such a thing.—Mr. Greenall : Is the house Atir own P—Defendant : Yes, I built it myself. I never knew a movable house wanted a certificate.—Mr. Long: You must let all the people at the works know about it. —Defendant was ordered to pay 4s ed, the costs.

AeCIDENT AT" MOORE. An accident occurred on the Moore section of the works on Tuesday morning. Iti.seems that a platelayer named Michael McMahon (35), was engaged in raising a road, when he was struck on tile head with a lever,-the blow rendering him uncenscicks for several minutes. Dr. Cannell, who happened to be in the neighbourhood at the time, was sent for, and he at once attended the injured man, who was subsequently removed to his lodgings on Town Hill, Warrington. The injury is not of a serious nature, and it is expected that MCMahon will resume work in about a fortnight,

div.head: SHIP CANAL WORKS,
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL WORKS,
• AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.

No 11.—THE CANAL NEAR. TRELWALL. A few short niehths ago a pedestrian on his way from Warrington to the ancient village:! Thelwall, after passing Morris Brook farm-house had on either hand as quiet a scene as any lover of rustic solitude could desire. To the left the meadows and ploughed land fell away in no great irregularity of surface to We southern banks of the Mersey and the view was only broken by the hedgerows inter- spersed with scattered trees. This piece of country has now, however, been invaded by the navvy and steam navvy and in place of picturesque old Eng- lish hedgerows, we have close at hand wooden erections, useful but unornamental, and piles of timber and other material, while two or three hun- dred yards away there is rapidly rising up a large elongated pile of brown earth which is being dug out of what is in future to be part of the channel of the great canal. Let us in anticipation of the work of the navvy, draw a picture of the changes the canal will work in this particular locality. BETWEEN LATCHFORD LOCKS AND TH4 MERSEY. As we have before explained the widening of the canal for Latchford Locks begins almost opposite Alderman Pickmere's late residence off Thelwall- lane, and ends on the eastern side of Morris Brook farmhouse. For a considerable distance before reaching the lock from the west, the canal runs through a deep cutting, but at the loops the waters are raised some fifteen or sixteen feet, and, of course, maintain this higher level till the next of the series of locks on the inland side. Between the Latchford Locke and the bank of the Mersey to the north of Thelwall not only is the water of the canal at a higher level than at any point we have yet touched upon, but the natural level of the ground is considerably lower than through Stockton Heath and Latchford, where we have seen the deep cut- tings are to be made. Indeed, between the locks of the Mersey at Thelwall the natural level of the ground only at one point rises ten feet above the intended level of the canal, while in other parts, and especially towards the river, it sinks as low as the intended level of the canal. EMBANKMENTS AT THELWALL. It is obvious, therefore, that along this stretch some embanking will be necessary, and as a matter of fact, whenever the ground is less than ten feet above the canal ft is intended to raise embankments to that height, set that at no place on the section we are considering will the waters Of the canal be at less than ten feet from the top of its enclosing bank. These embankments, or part of the embank- ments, will, it may be supposed, be visible from the Warrington and Thelwall-road, and it will certainly be a prominent object when viewedfrom the front entrance door of Thelwall Hall, the residence of Mr. James Nicholson, and hence we find certain provi- sions in that part of the Canal Company's Act de- voted to the protection of the interests of Mr. Nicholson. A clause states that the company shall construct and finish the embankments of so much of the canal as lies between a joint ,almost midway between Morris Brook and the Mersey, and is visi- ble from the front entrance door of Thelwall Hall in accordance with certain specified sections of plans. It is further provide& that Mr. Nicholson may re- quire the company to increase the height of the em- bankments to any reasonable extent, and that tee portion of the embankment on the south side of the canal shall be levelled, turfed, and finishes to ythe reasonable satisfaction of Mr. Nicholson, so as to present as sightly and natural an appearance as pos- sible, and "shall be so maintained and kept by the company at all times hereaf*, and shall if and when required by the said lames Nicholson be planted with trees or shrubs to the reasonable satis- faction of the said *James Nicholson and enclosed with a suitable fence." INTERSECTED ROADS. Between Latchford Locks and the Mersey the canal will intersect two roadways, one of which branches att. the left from the Warrington and Thelwall road about midway between Morris Brook farmhouse and Thelwall village and comes.to an end in some fields; the other and more important one branches off to the left in the centre of the village and running towards the north skirts the bank of the Mersey. For the preservation of the first- named roadway we know of no provision, and it will probably in future reach an abrupt termina- tion on the southerly bank of the canal. For the other road, however—that leading directly ot4 of the village—the company are to provide, and for ever maintain, a ferry across the canal suitable for all descriptions of vehicular traffic and for carrying fifteen ton loads, and also to furnish all the labour and power necessary to work this ferry by night and by day. Pr per and convenient approaches are to be made to the ferry on both sides; the roads having gradients of zio less than one in thirty. WHARVES. Near this farry there will be a wharf or landing • place on each side of the canal, at which the neigh- bouring owners of land and their tenants and ser- vants are to be at liberty to embark and land free from wharfage rates, various materials to be used for the cultivation of the soil, but the right of using these wharves is to be subject to reasonable *bye- laws, from time to time made by the canal company and siibject to the approvil of the Board of Trade. A SDGGESTED ROAD. It will have been gathered from what has been Said in previous articles that a vehicle starting from Thelwall along the present road to' Warrington will, in, order to reach the latter place, have to branch off to the left past the front of Morris Brook farmhouse, and go along the new road that is to be made on the south bank of the canal till he reaches Knuts- ford-road, *here he may pass over the swing bridge and 'then take a straight course to Warrington. There is, however, in the Act of Parliament some indication of an alternative route from Thelwall on the north side of the canal. It is stated, "for the protection of" Mr. John Vigor Fox of Girsby Manor, Lincoln, an owner of land in the neighbour- hood of Thelwall, that the canal company shall, if required by Mr. FOX, construct, within certain specified limits of deviation, and contemporane- ously with the ferry referred to above, and for ever after maintain, a road twenty-one feet wide along thg northerly side of the canal from the ferry in a westerly direction- to the boundary between the townships of Thelwall and Grappenhall. This road is projected for the purpose of forming a means of access and communication between lands on the north side of the canal, and Mr. Fox, his tenants and workmen, and all persons acting on his or' their behalf, are to he entitled, free from all.dues and charges, to pass and repass along the road. It is also stated that should the canal company con- ptruct a cart road, which will be a continuation of the above, mentioned road, along the north bank of the canal- to the nearest swing bridge in the parish of Grappenhall, Mr. Fox, his tenants, &c., are to have a similar right of using this road. It should be mentioned that when the roads named have been made they are to, be subject to the use• of other neighbouring land owners such as the vicar of Holy , Trinity Church, Warrington, owner for the time ,being of glebe land and property on the north of the canal, Mr. John Buckley, of. New Delph, and Mr. Henry Stanton, of Greenfield House, Thelwall. THE LANDOWNERS PROTECTED. It will have been seen that the land in the neigh- bourhood of Thelwall is to be very considerably cut up and dislocated, and it is only natural that the landowners should seek to protect themselves as far as possible from pecuniary and other injury. We find, consequently, in addition to the' provisions mentioned above, that almost in all cases, the Canal Company are to pay to the owners compensation for any depreciation caused to their lands by reason of any interference by the company. div.head: ALLEGED SUNDAY DRINKING.
div.p: ALLEGED SUNDAY DRINKING.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, before the Mayor (Alderman Sut- telt) and other magistrates, Mrs. Mary Ellen Kier- nan, landlady of the Patten Arms hotel, was sum- moned for having, on the morning'of Sunday, the 18th instant, uglawfullY sold intoxicating liquors to Worg.e BircHall, who was himself summoned for having been on licensed premises during prohibited hours. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the defence, and pleaded not guilty. Evidence was given by P.C. Monaghan, whose statement vas corroborated by" P.C. Dean, to the effect that at 10-30 on the morning in question the officers were passing along Parker- street when they notices that a side door, leading to the Patten Arms tap, was open. They went to tie bar, and saw defendant Birchall drinking beer out of a glass. .The barman was inside the bar, and another man was standing close at hand. The berme' told the officer that the glass of beer had been left on the previous day for Birchall, and, as they were leaving the'premises, Birchall said," I have helped him to brush up, and he has given Me that". In answer to Mr. Davies, Constable Monaghan said that he saw no money passed. Birchall was one of the tenants of the Patten Arms stables. The •barman did .not say that Birchall had a glass of beer every Sunday morning for helping him to wash up the bar.—Mr. Davies said that to him the case seemed to be a very trivial one. Had the men been outsiders there might have been some grounds for the action. Mr. Birchall and a Mr. Parker were tenants of the Patten Arms stables, and Birchall, it was admitted, had a glass of beer every Sunday morning.—The Mayor.: I think that if you bring us evidenoe that the man was working there in the manner described it will be sufficient.—The defendant Birchall was then sworn. He said that he went to the stables at seven o'clo& on the morning in question, and had done certain woirk for the barman. He had been in the habit of having a glass of beer.. there on a Sunday morning for a long time.—The Mayor said that to the Bench it seemed that there had been no inten- tion to break the law. Refreshments had simply been given to a servant. He thought that it was rather strain- ing at the law to attempt to carry it out in that way. They should dismiss the case.—The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said that the defendant Birchall was not employed as a servant at the Patten Arms. The police happened to be passing the place, and reported things as they found them. Mr. Parker was registered as a cab proprietor, but Mr. Birchall was not. The Mayor said that the Bench had had evidence that he was in some measure employed as a servant.—The Chief-constable: He is not a servant at all.—The Mayor: Wethink he was employed in some way.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. H. B. White) said that in such cases the onus of proof was thrown upon the defendant.—Alderman Harrison said that the police had been right in the action that they had taken, but the evidence did not reveal an amount of culpability that would justify the Bench in convicting.—The 'Mayor also said that the Bench did not wish to say anything against the police, who had been right in bringing the matter forward.—Both cases were then dismissed.

- - _ THE TRADESMEN a WARRINGTON. Sir,—l have been taking your valuable -paper In for some considerable time. On Saturday last my attention was drawn for the first time to a letter signed by " Member." Now, sir, I ask the writes to name those tradesmen he accuses of dishonest practices, and prove the accuracy of his statements, or else make a public apology to the tradesmen he slanders, 4.1R4 to yourself for taking up your valuable time and space. I have been in a few towns, but nowhere have I been served better cheaper, oz more honestly than by the Warring- ton tradesmen, grocers included. Thanking you for year kindness in affording space for this, I am, dear sir, yours truly, GEORGE 'I:VRAFIAM.•

150, Hoyle-street. B'4- THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION. Sir.—l cannot profess to feel any great admiration for Bellerophon's" acuteness of insight. Me comes to con- 'elusions very rapidly, hut his conclusions seem to be in- variably wrong. Oa the strength of /my last letter he accuses me of being ." an ygly development" of the lyssus teetotaller. But as a matter of fact I have either net de- veloped far enough sr develeped too far to be of that genus, and it is clear that " Bellerophon " is weak in his powers of classification. What struck •me in his TtrA later , was the singnlarabsurthy of his era declaring *at he hated drunk:it-mess, andlihen railing incoherentlyagainst those who wish te do away with the thing he hates. He will perhapsstry that it is the method of the teetotallers —their " meddling with other people's concerns "—he objects to. but this puts him in a still more isdiculous, and irrational position. He agrees with their aim, -which is the removal of drunkenness, but with a mud- ' died (I will ret say fuddled for, " Bellerophon" seems I' to be a thin-skinned critic) incom4stelcy which is, per- ' 'haps, not alt of phase in a champion of the liquor trade, : he mali,gnstitem for adopting the most effective methdd of carryieg out their purpose, and method 'which le resorted to whenever legislation ef any kind takes place. Your correspondent appears to resent .being classed -with the Nihilists (or - Anarchists, but one xnust reason from the known to the unknown. He made known kis antipathy to "other people's concerns" beingineddled with, and from this one naturally concluded that be belonged to that sattion of politicians who make this point the cat(Enal article in their creed. But I can quite believe after reading his letters that' Bellerophon" has no eery defined political principles, either Anarchist or otherwise, and that it is only somee people's concerns that he does wilt liketo be meddled with am, sir,

Wangton, Maxch 28,1288. Sir,—l shall feel obliged if you will allow me to say a few words on this question, which at the present -seems to be agitatingthe minds of the public somewhat. lam in favour of total abstinence myself, but I must confess to a .feeling of diseust at the attitude of some of the pro- fessed teetotallers of Warrington, who seem to go about their work of reform by fits and starts, and in a manner altogether half-hearted. last at present, no doubt, after the incentive given them by Mr. Justice Granthana, they feel very fine and largo, and are prepared to push the war into the enemy's camp to any ,extent short of trying to meddle with the rich and powerful brewers, more or less rich end powerful according to the quantity of the " cursed drink" they manufacture. It is all very well to abuse and condemn the publican, but is he,, the man who sells liquor, any worse than the other (me, who makes it for him to sell? Teetotallers seem ready enough to condemn the publicans, and the traffic itself, but then Sir Gilbert Greenall, for instance, can not very well be condemned. No.; certainly not. The publican serves his customers with the beer Sir Gilbert grows rich through, but Sir Gilbert himself drives his carriage and pair, and writes M.P. after his name. Nay, more, he gives money to the church, and the church with one hand held up in righteous indignation at the horrid trade, with the other hand smilingly and thankfully receives a portion of the gains of that horrid trade. To me it seems in this case that if the publicans touch pitch they are defiled: but if a brewer touches pitch he is not defiled—wit by any means. The more he does in that way and the more he increases his hoard the better he is liked, especially by the sycophants of the church. Brewers and publicans are in the saline vessel, but the breweris rich enough to pay dock-dues to enter the port of respecta- bility and social honour, while the publican, being but a humble servant of "his nibs" aforesaid, is comparatively- a poor man, and has to remain tossing about on the sea of degradation, from which his partner has so luckily escaped. Should not this state of things be reversed? If blame attaches to those engaged in the traffic, and if they are to be held responsible for its evil consequencee. surely a brewer in a tremendous way of business has far -snore to answer for than many publicans.—Yours, &c., H. Warrington, March 30, 1888.

WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE STORES. was not at all surprised to see that, by writing 5n support of the above, I had drawn upon myself the fire of the heavy artillery belonging to the Warrington army of grocers, but I am happy to say that 'I have es- caped entire annihßation. Well, sir, let me say that in my last, a clerical error made me state per quarter in- stead of per week at the end of my figures. and that it did not need a schoolmaster to see the error. lam not going to deal at great length with some of the milk-and-water arguments of my three opponents, simply because my time is too valuable to waste in such a manner; but I will make time to assure them that the schoolmaster is at home and not abroad, the greatest pity being the fact that he might have been abroad in' my young days, for aught I khow, through my haying to part company at the advanced age of eightyears, to earn my own salt at the highlyesalted trade of fustian cutting. Will, when the necessity arises, I can quote many others besides Carlyle, though I have "patted rozine " in the form of a tomnsy shop," as a netessary adjunct to my course of education. So much for the good breeding of one who evidently knows little about the trust shops to 1 which I refer.

• ti) Looker On," I can assure him that we Ad use some of the articles he names, and we pay a cer- tain price to get a proper article, as shown by the re- marks of a member in your issue of the 24th ; and I as- sure a "Looker On" that I appreciate his sarcastic re- marks re halfpenny checks; it is really better medicine than Beechara's noted pills. Another of your correspondents reminds me of many noted political characters by carefully letting my chief arguments alone, and proceeds to distort 25 in the pound into 3s 2d, and then asks where the remainder goes after paying the " divi." Now, sir, I have had a wash and my breakfast since I wakened this morning, and am too wide-awake to answer that question further than refer him to my remarks as to our sound position, contenting myself with assuring him that we. could even pay 30s to the pound if wound up to-day, thanking him also for the margin of profits he gives us, which, I feel sure, will not receive an echo from many of his brother tradesmen. Turning to the ordinary trust shop, lam aware that in many cases you may meet with genuine kindness, and lam sorry to see that even the proprietor of one should have been treated in such a disgraceful manner, after - lending out hard gash, and I trust the happy possessor of so benevolent a disposition will improve in his ability to \ judge character for the future. The class of trust shops to which I refer are those situated in the quieter parts of the town, the keepers of which calmly (to use a figure of speech) take the measure of all tge people in their immediate neighbourhood, and, after fishing out the ap- parent safe ones, they in some way remind them theyca,n , have anything they want and "pay just as you like, you know." These are the class of business people who charge equal to the Stores, and would almost be offended if you did not owe them a sovereign or two, simply be- causefifteen or a score customers are a living, while the smallldebt is a kind of millstone. I for one have done with this, and prefer the Stores; and when I want hard cash I fetch it. It is a poor soul who could not soon allow more than he could borrow to stand to his credit in twelve months. At least I have found it so, though we are seven, and I put something by from only 45 per day. —I remain, sir, yours truly, '
ONE WHO KNOWS.

A VISIT TO INCE,

The 'progress of the works being ilone on this section is rerrnarkable. During the last three weeks an enor- rseous quantity of plant has arrived, and,.uotwith.stond- ing the opposition which has been shown towards' the contractor as to right of road, the work goes merrily on, under the very able superintendence of Mr. Brown, who has charge of this section. Already there are three steam navvies, three. locomotives, three steam cranes, and three portable engines, and a very large quantity of other material on the meadows near Mr. HassalPs farm. face wharf, by the river, is covered with plant isf various kind. This wharf has been found very useful. A steam saw mill has been kept busy at work cutting up boards, and already'lto less than eight dwelling huts have been erected and made comparatively corillertable for their tenants. The butcher's shop and stores is al- most finished, arid,a'number of other huts are being. erected. Complaints are nu.de by tlid tenants as to the'. non delivery of letters. - These dwellins are `Wing put up on the canal land, and near the river -where there have not been any dwellings. They are abont a man from the village of Ince, and the postman requires fresh officialiinstructious. No doubt the matter will be put right shortly.. Blacksmiths' shop with forges, fitters' shop for repairs, joiners' shop, and large 'offices are being erecthd ; while water tanks are being fixed to supply the engines and for other parposes. I large number of wag- gons have arrived, andthe engines are, busy taking soil and clay in= the cuttings to form the embankments. The navvies are at work removing the top soil with spades and barrows, and pitting it away for future use. Lines of rails are laid down in various directions, -and al- together about 500 men are 'busy near Ince. I large number of men are at work at Stanlow Point, and before long there will be asils laid all the way from Eastham to Flodsham Marsh, a distaneeei ten males. RUNCORN.

The work of cut Eng the canal on this section is pro- gressing very rapialy, as there are now four American navvies in use. The snow that fell on Tuesday night and Wednesday morning impeded operations, but not to any serious extent, and the excavations are of consider- able depth and great length. Through the treacherous nature of the marsk, Mr. Gregson has had some difficulty in laying the spoil bank; but there has been no diminu- tion in the immense deposits of clay, thanks to the skill and ingenuity of the engineering navvy. Preliminary steps are being taken for cominencing operations in the river. Several men are engaged daily in taking exten- sive and minute observations of the rise and fall of the tide, so that the engineers will be the better enabled to deal with the immense volume of water, when the im- portant work a pile-driving, kc., is commenced. The whdle of the men employed on the section stopped work for the Easter holidays on Thursday at noon, and will not resume until Tuesday morning next. THEL WALL. Yesterday work was suspended on the Thelwall sec- tion of the canal, though notwithstanding the incle- mency of the day, the locality was visited by a consider- able number of sightseers. These, however, for the most part were not permitted to go near the works which, in- deed, were encompassed with mud, and notices caution- ing trespassers, have been posted up. The offices which, as we have before mentioned, have for some time been in course of erection, are now quickly approaching com- pletion, and the framework of a considerable number of huts for the workmen has already been put up. A num- ber of locomotives are now in full operation, and it is tobe noticed that a steam navvy of the" American" type has been placed in one of the cuttings. Other steam navvies are in course of erection. A temporary, but substantial bridge to connect both sides of the river will, judging from appearances, soon be opened, when the workings on either side will doubtless be connected by a line of metals. On the north side of the river the work of excavating for both the canal and the new bed iof the river, which s to be diverted at this point, is in full swing, and Wildegrave farmhouse is almost hidden from view by the growing embankments. ACCIDENT AT LYMM. On Tuesday morning an accident took place on the' Lymm section of the canal. A joiner who was engaged in the erection of huts for the labourers, fell from the top of one of the buildings and sustained somewhat serious injuries to the head and other parts of the body.

div.head: ECCLES AND BARTON.
div.p: ECCLES AND BARTON.

Great anxiety prevails on the Eccles (Trafford sub- section) and Barton section. On Monday.aftetnoon a number of stalwart navvies were engaged m unloading from a at a prodigious steam navvy, nick-named by the men "The American devil." It was brought up the river from Latchford, and has been used in the works necessitated by the Ribble scheme at Preston. It is capable of scooping out and lifting Newt. of earth at each stroke. At Trafford Park a number of men are erecting hoardings to mark the boundary of the canal, and large quadtities of timber continue to arrive by boat. Mr. Leader Williams went over the section in company with Mr. Walkers the contractor, on Monday morning. At present there alb 55 men engaged on this section at so much per day, and 88 men who are paid on piece at the rate of 4d per yard of earth re- moved. Crowds of visitors continue to watch the pro- gress of the works, and each new arrival of machinery proves a source of much interest. The men ceased work on Thursday for Easter holidays, resuming nest Tues. day, a notice to this effect being posted in the various sections. At Peelgreen men are employed in advance of the steam digger. Massive embankments of sods and earth are being piled up by spade and barrow work, a "spit," over a foot thick, being taken off the adjoining grass land, the navvies earning from 4s 6d to 5s per day. Quantities of material continue to arrive by rail and river. Mr. McGrath is the agent for the Barton section, and Mr. Rainor the sub-agent.

RUNCORN v. BRADFORD. , The return match between these teams at Runcorn on Saturday aroused a large amount of interest, and when the ball was set rolling there could not have been less than 3,500 persons present within the enclosure. Owing to the late arrival of the visitors two "thirties" only were played, during which period one of thefinest games ever played in the district was witnessed. Shortly after 4 p.m. H. Hughes, as captain, kicked off on be- half of Runcorn, and after some smart exchanges in the centre, Brazendale kicked beautifully within the Bradford half. Although the visitors now had the ad- vantage of a fM, kick, the homesters rushej the ball to the Bradford line, and after a short but birited .yuR 1 illVhitby gained a brilliant try, front wLich'Brazendale I failed at goal. Shortly after the re-start Ritchie passed Ito Robertshaw, who made headway until Haneock inter- posed near touch, and scrimmaging was brought about in neutral ground. The pack flaying broken up, the Cheshiremen broke away in a splendid dribble. Stubbs, Hancock, Wainwright, and Hughes Being prominent in the raid. Hawcridge ultimately checked the attack, whereupon the visitors dashed off in unisoneand a mo- ment later Bonsor scored near the post, but without re- sult. A free kick by Wilkinson was strategetically used, but nothinv came of it. Although directly afterwards Ritehie paZed to Hawcridge, who ran in splendidly, no I goal, however, resulting from Hickson's kick. From the dropout Dolan cleared the Runcorn half, and in close fol- lowing Brazendale got rid of the ball in capital style, but I although Hawcridge obtained a free kick, Brazendale rendered further service to his side. Haigh relieyed, whereupon Hawcridge carried on the ball, scrimmaging being again brought about within the home 25. Wil- kinson now took the oval grandly on lining out, and from a subsequent rush the ball was consigned to the forwards, right in front of the Runcorn goal, on the break up of which half-time was called, with the Nisi- tors leading by two tries to one, the play so far hading been exciting in the extreme. .Hickson restarted, and. after a brief period of central play, Faulkner obtained a free kick, from which a rush was made for the Bradford line. 'Ritchie relieved at the corner, and the 25 having been cleared Hickson dashed from the pack with the ball at his toes in magnificent style. Bonsor now be- came particularly prominent, but so vigorous wie the defence that the Yorkshiremen were brought to bay at the n 'yards' line. Here repeated scrimmages were waged, until Faulkner broke away, only to have the ball removed to midfield a moment later, Wood I shortly afterwards relieving in good style. Brazendale also put in a serviceable kick, and in the run over the line Faulkner, Sydney Critchley, fortunately for his r side, kicked dead over the heads of the crowd. From a further free kick Brazendale punted across' and vigor- ous play ensued on the Runcorn 'left, until from a simi- lar advantage by Faulkner, Brazendale made a grand attempt at goal, a minor ensuing, although cheers were raised on the presumption that a goal had been dropped. It was a near thing, however, and with its failure, the chances of a home victory, to the relief of the Bradfor- dians. were seriously diminished. Still for a while the visitors were pressed, but at length Bonsor dashed gal- lantly to mid-field, P. Riley's tackling powers at this juncture being brolight into play, with the most advan- tageous results. Some grand punting and passing was now shown by both sides, but although the Runcorn- ian theys continued unable tot o have improve3ligthhtellry the bt score, and df eventually play, a magnificently contested game, in which:the be of good humour prevailed, terminated in favour of Bradford by two tries to a try and two minor points—Teams: Run- corn: T. Wood', back ; .H. Cawley, J. Brazendale, and ,W. A. Riley, three-quarter-backs ; H. Hughes and G. Whitby, halkoacks ; W. H. Broady, W. Faulkner, W. Hughes, G. Wainwright. J. Clarke, W. Stubbs, R. Dolan, P. Riley, and F. Hancock, forwards. Bradford: Haigh, back; F. T. Ritchie, E. Critchley, and J. J. Hiw- cridge, three-qUarter-backs I P. Bonsor and S. Critch- lev, half-backs; E. Wilkinson, Potter, H. Robertshaw, Higgins, W. Gray, J. Fisher, L. Hickson, H. Jowett, and J. Toothill, forwards.

WEST AANCASHIRE CHALLENGE CUP COMPETITION. FINAL TIE •AT WARRINGTON. ANOTHER ACCOUr. A Widnes correspondent writes with regard to the match :—Although the ground and surroundings at War- rington are most suitable for a match of this nature, the

div.head: TIIE EXAMINER SATURDAY-, MARCH -31, 1888._
div.p: TIIE EXAMINER SATURDAY-, MARCH -31, 1888._

Widnes team journeyed to the battle ground !a-anything but favourable spirits, and it is believed by many of their ardent supporters, that their defeat -and discomfi- ture were attributable to the action of the Rugby Asso- ciation in ignoring the appeal of the Widnes Committee ' to have the locality changed. . However, it Was neces- sary to accept the inevitable and make the best of it. Punctually to time the teams entered the arena, each re- ceiving the hearty plauditS of their friends assembled round the enclosure. Precisely at 3-30, Smith, having won the toss, and having elected to play with the sun at his back,Tyldesley kicked ,amidst the intense and pent up excitement of the interested spectators. The ball, not being returned, play settled in the Widnes quarters, and the game had not proceeded far, when, after a scrimmage, the ball was kicked towards the Widnes line, and Hughes happening to touch the ball, it put lodgkinson, who was considerably in front of his_ own men, on side, and he, taking advantage, fell en the ball. and secured a good but exceedingly lucky try, from which Shaw (the captain) placed an easy goal. This piece of luck inspired the Tyldesley men with increased courage, and also roused the Wideesians to their work, the play becoming faster and more spirited. Each side now was in earnest, and apparently bent on e.ace;ting it-. self to its utmost capacity, the balltravelling first in one direction, and then the ether. As sure as one side gained any ground, it was as surely retrieved by the other -Pby still raged in the Widnes half, Farrell's collaring and saving being superb, till at length Hard:. man and Parkinson worked the hall, and followed up te. beyond mid-field. Wilkinson, receiving from a pass, now got along, and, failing to put in his kick ortmasfer, was quickly brought to bay. Give and take seemed now thre order of the day. Plempten, snaking a fair catch, the ball was carried into Tyldeeley 25. Barker passed to Wilkinson, who kicked towards goal, and Far- rell, smartly following up, held the Tyldesley man close to the posts,- biff danger was soon averted. Tall kicking on the part of the backs, re- suiting in frequent tree kicks, took place on boat sides, but neither side could brea'k through the alray defended lines. The ball was once , kicked over the Widnes line, but Phunpton ran round and returned the ball into play beyond the 25 flag. for , which piece of work he was loudly cheered. Barker obtaining, had a clear run before him, but the whistle called him back. Wilkinson, taking a flying kick, gained a lot of ground, which was further ipaproved by the for- wards; but Tyldesley proved equal to the occasion, and prevented disaster, half-time being now called with Tyldesley a goal to Widnes nil. • After the interval Smith kicked off from the centre, and the ball being returned Hughes was collared before he could do anything. ; Pearson with a fine kick, sent the ball to near theWid- nes goal, where Farrell obtained a free kick for off-sidel tackling. Anther free kick by Plumpton removed I hostilities to centre. Bingham, inakirig a feeble return, , the ball went into touch in the Widnes quarter, and from the line out the ball was kicked over the Widnes line, a minor point being conceded_ The ball, from the drop out, was carried into Tyldesley territory, but Ramsden relieved by a good run, being pushed into touch. Kiddie obtaining a fair catch, Plumpton took the place, making a good shot for goal, but the ball just strudk a Tyldesley forward and checked its progress. Parkinson, from a flying kick, sent the ball over the Tyldesley line, which necessitated a touchdown, the only point that Widnes scored throughout the game. Shortly after the drop out, the Tyldesley men, following up quickly, took the ball again near the Widnes line, and Bingham failing to pick "up a Tyldesley man attempted to touch the ball down, but Hardman fortunately was just in time to kick dead. Tyldesley claimed a try* but the referee decided that the ball had not been made station- ary. Hardman and Smith showed prominently in a dribble. More exchanges took place in the way of free kicks, till at length the ball was kicked dead again over the Widnes line.

..... The Widnes men now worked desperately to score and were seen to more advantage than at any other parts of the game, and when it seemed likely that they might equalise matters, the fatal whistle sounded the conclusion of the final struggle for supremacy, leaving Tyldesley the lucky victors by 9 points to 1. It was a grandly contested game, the teams being very evenly matched. It was particularly conspicuous for fine and tall kicking, in fact it was a treat to see I many of the huge punts that sent the ball from one end I of the field to the other. It is much'more interesting to I witnsss this loose play than the eternal rough and tom- We scrimmages, that usually attend cup contests. Berry showed up most conspicuously for Tyldesley, but e,a,ch one played in grand style. For Widnes, Farrell and Plumpton shone most, whilst Hardman, Smith, and Wilkinson were occasionally to the fore.

iDEMPERANCE -PARTY AND TIM '.4. LOCAL O,OVERNILENT BILL. . . . _ special meeting of the National Temperance Feciera- %ken, comprising delegates from 24 leading national tem- perance organisations, was held on Tuesday, in Exeter' gall, London, under the preside,ncy a -Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P. who was supported by Messrs. M•Lagan and Wil- son, members of Parliament. The main subject dis- cussed was the licensing proposals of the Local Govern- ment Bill. Mr. M`Lagan, M.P., proposed the first reso- lution—" 'Mat the,proposed traiiisfer of lieeftsing powers to bodies elected on general issues in no way meets the desire of the temperance party, but is calculated to so complicate matters as to prove even more unsatis- factory than the present licensing system.' The resolntion was carried unanimously. Further resolutions were proposed. The first protested against the transfer of license revenues to local bodies, as creating corporate interest in the perpetuation and , extension of the drink traffic, which, whilst seeming to, confer upon the ratepayers present pecuniary advantage, would really render the evils of the traffic more than evgr diffietilt to cope with. The second declared that the burdens of the drink traffic entitle the people to the right of extinguishing the source of such evils, and that the people in localities should have local power by direct -vote .to prevent the establishment or continuance of drink'shops. The third noted with satisfaction that practically all the temperance organisations of the Uni- ted• Kingdom have declared against any compensation being due to publicaes on the discontinuance of licenses, and resolved to offer. strertious opposition to the com- pensation clauses in the Local Government Bill en the ground that a license to sell intoxicants is granted for one year and no longeir, but that the superior courts have repeatedly ruled that a license- bolder has no vested interest in a license, and that it has teen repeatedly held that the licensing authorities have the same power to refuse to re-license a public-house as they have to refuse to license any neva applicant, and that no claim has ever existed for compensation in case of any such refusal. The fourth is to the effect that, having considered the Gover9ment proposals in relation to the liquor traffic as set forth in the Local Government Bill, the federation deliberately declared that the said proposals are calculatedto delay and distract and pre- vent just and righteons legislation upon the matter, and merit heavy condemnation.—Mr. Caine proposed that eopies of the resolutions should be sent to every member of both Houses of Parliament, which was agreed to. A council meeting of the United Kingdom Alliance having met in the afternoon and passed resolutions also strongly condemning the Government proposals, a joint meeting of the two bodies was held in the evening to concert joint action in opposition to compensation and in support of direct veto. ,

THE CLERICAL SCANDAL.—LETTER FROM MRS. BREAKENRIDGE. The following letter appeared last week in the 'Eccles and Patricroft Journal ": Dear sir,—At the cost of much pain to myself, I feel compelled, now that I have sufficiently regained my strength, to undertake the task to ask you to kindly allow me to correct some of the many inaccurate and misleading statements that have been circulated about my unhappy daughter, the loss of whom has entailed upon myself and family such endless and irrepressible misery. Much that is incorrect and unjust has been said of the Is of Man incident. My daughter went there by agreement, signed and accepted two months previously, to sing at twelve morning concerts; she had then no knowledge that Mr. and Mrs. Mules intended going there, but it was at their united and strongly pressed invitation that my daughter and I agreed to occupy the same apartments along with another mutual lady friend. I was with illy daughter the whole of the time from leaving to returnino. to Eccles, and I never saw what might be construed as the slightest excess of attention on the part of Mr. Mules towards her. I have made it an infallible rule to either accompany her to concerts myself or to send one of her sisters with, her, except in her London engagements, and then she was in the hands of relatives, which I also anticipated would be the case at the fatal concert at Southport, when both she and I fully expected that her aunt and uncle, who reside in that neighbourhood, would be present according to promise, and to whose house she was invited to stay over night. We have a letter now in our possession, written by her to her uncle, giving evidence that she expected him to be there. Surely, then, it is impossible thaf she could have planned to go to America the following day. With regard to her portmanteau, I have positivepersonal knowledge that it contained only a okicert dress and such little necessaries as would be required for one or ' two nights' visit at the utmost. Nor has she, as it has been stated; had any article whatever sent on to her. I

_ may also say that I went with her to Eccles Station, where we found that she was too We ler the train by which eie intended travelling, and ednSeqUently we had to wait for the next. These and many other facts, as well as my own intuitive consciousness, which nothing can shake, are conclusive evidences that she had no knowledge that she was leaving me for the last time. She was ever to me a loving, simple, and confiding daughter, and I leave it to those who knew her to judge if she could be guilty of this ap- palling sin unless she had been duped and decoyed by the wicked man who, in the garb of sacred office, has destroyed her, robbed me of my child, and therefore con- signed me and my fatherless children to lifelong sorrow. In refutation of charges that I have been cognisant of .and even encouraged his attentions, I cab only say that on hearing of the scandal some time back I requested him to discontinue his visits to my house/ and more than that, I gave notice that I and my family should leave his church, whereupon he most solemly declared that he I had no more regard for my unfortunate daughter than he he had for any of her sisters, and he protested strongly that I should increase the scandal to his injury if I adopted the course named. After such ayow?.ls I felt almost ashamed of suspecting him to any de,gree what- ever. I have received many letters and usurau.oes from friends who knew my daughter pure-minded and simple nature,. testilyi4 to her ancl. "her ever-rOnstant hope of excelling in her P:ofelsion in order to recom- pense me for the sP- t'a which her musical 'education exacted. W al'ett; thdet sacrifices have been I kave others ,te 'judge. She el-Wiled under the best of wastes who predicted for ter dt bright-future. She earned food fees and her engr.g•ements were rapidly multiplying. It was her greate•At pleasure to help me in supporting my some- what nuancrons family. The Almighty, in His wisdom, hass4'it fit to take my treasure from me, and in Ms ~.`-'nr.nipetent Hand I must leave my wrong and my child. - .Ay Wiore, to Him, too, I must leave the author and chief actor in this iniquity. I have composed this letter from a bed of illness, from which at one time it was considered irApossible that I could recover,in the hope that it may infusethe light of 'truth into the criticisms that such a Calamity inevitably produces. Apologising for occupying so much of your space, I am, yours faithfully, Ellesmere-road, Eccles, March 22nd, 1888.
N. A. BREAKENRIDOE.

With the terutination of the sedDentent, business for all practical purposes has come to t Conclusion until after the Easter lsaktrys, and it will not he before the middle of next week that anything like active business will be resumed. The I settieraem, just concluded has been, with the exception of one or twe special markets, a particularly light one, and the influ- encetf the settlement with the approaching holiday was very apparent even at the close of last week. Mr. Goschen's Budget has naturally been the staple subject ef conversation in the City during the past two days and its leading proposals are generally aceppted, although ;here are -one or two features to which steady men might take an objection. The chief of these is the shilling per cent, on bonds and shares to bearer. It is not so much the proposal itself, but the difficulty of putting it into force, added to the already involved system of the various stamp duties. Mr. Goschen would- be doing a service to investors if he would devote some attention to simplifying the involved intricacies ' and the delays caused by the present cumbersome method of transfers. ' The reduction of a penny in the iecome tax is naturally popular, and Mr. Goschen's own-popularity in the city is suf- ficient to secure a favourable reception for his proposals. The one feature which seems to cause some irritation among city men is the increase of sixpence for the stamp for contract notes. and Mr. Goschen will evidently have to alter his pro- posal. Home rails continue in steady demand. We called atten- tion some few weeks ago to Brighton A's, recommending them as a good investment and, contrary to opinion, a specu- lation for a rise. The present quotation is sufficient justifica- tion for what we then said. To-day Brighton A's stand over 116. When we recommended them they were 112. The gamble still continues in De Beers, and indications are still wanting that the anticipated rapid fall in th4e shares is close at hand. A number of 'bears' sold on the hope that at the last settlement prices would be much lower. As a matter of fact, they were made up even higher than a fortnight pre-. viously. • Gold mining shares have been adversely-affected, andthere is scarcely any speculation in this field at present. Inaian mining shares were regarded as certain for an early rise. The sudden- and unexpected death of Mr. William Ab- bott, who might have been called the pioneer of this company. had an adverse influence upon them for a day or two, but there are indications that the rise he anticipated in them will ultimately come about. For the next week it would be useless to even suggest any- thing either for investment or speculation. Our readers would do well to simply ignore Stock Exchange matters for an.ther week unless they happen to be holders of Russian ' 73's, which we strongly urge them to sell at present prices, which are firm, and perhaps nearly the best they are likely to see for some time.

"The Life of Burns" is published by Mr. Walter Scott in the Great Writers series. It iS from the pen of Mr. John Stuart Blackie, and it is in every respect an ad- 1 mirable work. It is seldom that'Burns gets strict justice; the writer either glozes over his faults and presents a phantom instead of a man, or magnifies his weaknesses and creates a monster. Mr. Blackie does neither the one nor the other; he nothing extenuates nor sets down aught in malice; and the result is that we see the poet as he was—a man of great genius and nobility of char- acter, but subject to passionate impulses, and altogether too convivial in a convivial age. The reader of this life will feel, after its perusal, that he knows Burns bet- ter, and despite his failings, that he admires him the more as "the man o' independent mind, and king o men for e that."

In the Canterbury Poets for March, we have the poeti- cal workaof Thomas Moore, selected and edited, with an introduction, by Mr. John Dorrian. A volume such as Ithis is especially welcome at a time when the Irish question excites so much interest.
