Great &mega has been done hi the neighbourhood of Wellington, and many miles of railway on the coast have been destroyed. Major John Haswell, commanding the Morpeth cotti- pany of the Northumberland Battalion of Fusileers, was found dead in a railway carriage at Newsham station , yesterday morning. The Rev. George Butt, M.A., Vicar of Chesterfield, died on Thursday morning at Chesterfield, in his seventy-third. year. The living is the gift of the Bishop of Southwell, and is valued at about £4OO per annum. • Owing to the representations made as to the extensive prevalence of small-pox in Sheffield, it is understood that all railway excursions to and from that town, inclusling those to Liverpool, have been withdrawn.' FATALITY AT A COLLIERY.—On Thursday morning Thos. Potter, a collier, was engaged removing timber from a root in the Peelwood colliery, Tyldesley, with three other men, wheq he was instantly killed. Decease:. was 57 years of age, and an experienced workman. The intended reduction in the price of coal in the Manchester district at the beginning of April is to be ac- companied by a reduction in colliers' wages to the extent of 10 per cent., that being the amount of the advance conceded by the masters on prices of coal being raised last January. _

• Darrntrevivs GALE.—On Thursday night a furious gale raged on the south-west coast of Ireland, compelling fishing boats to haul in nets and beat a hasty retrgat to the harbours. The skipper of one,boat was struck by the tiller and instantly killed. A number of boats were more or less damaged; one luggar was driven on the rocks at Baltimore and foundered, and a Newry boatlost her mizzen boom in the collision.

TUB FITZHATTRICE Muanza.—Commenting on the re- sult of the trial of the murderers of James Fitzmaurice, the " Freeman's Journal," while not wishing to question the justice of the verdict, says if ever there was a cause for Court of Criminal Appeal, this is one. Upon the evidence, Hayes has a case for further consideration, and it will be deplorable if he goes to the scaffold with- out some additional sifting and investigation of the charge.

div.head: HIGH SHERIFFS AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT
div.p: HIGH SHERIFFS AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT
BILL.

Lord Camperdown writes A committee has been appointed by the House of Lords to consider the mode of appointment of the duties and the obligations of High Sheriffs. The committee will meet immediately after the Easter recess. The courts of quarter sessions have it in their power to give valhable information to the com- mittee by taking this question into consideration at their meetings in next week. The office and duties of High Sheriff are closely connected with the question of Local Government, which will doubtless be disclissed by the magistrates. If it is concluded that changes with reference to the office of High Sheriff are desirable, the committee would like to know how, by whom, and at whose expense Her Majesty's -Judges are to be received when going on circuit, and how all the other duties of th# High Sheriff are to be discharged. As the mover for the committee, I write in hope that this letter may at- tract the attention of magistrates and of clerks of the peace.

RESIGNATION OF THE FRENCH GOVERNMENT. PARIS, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—The Chamber, to-day, despite the opposition of the Government, voted by a majority of thirty-one, urgency for a Bill brought in by the Extreme Left for the revision of the Constitution. The Government have therefore restgned.

THE EMPEROR FREDERICK. • BERLIN. FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—To-day for the first time since his acepsgion to the throne, the Emperor Frederick drove from Charlotenburg into Berlin and paid a visit to his mother. Enormous crowds collected along the route, and cheered His Majesty with the greatest enthu- siasm. • THE FLOODS IN GERMANY. - . .

• Further accounts of the disastrous floods in Germany show that the visitation has created terrible destruction, and Goosed much suffering over a wide area. In the vicinity of the Vistula alone seventy-seven villages are inundated, and 30.000 persons homeless. An area of ten German miles is flooded, and the pecuniary damage is estimated at many million marks. Many lives bave been lost. • THE CRISIS IN ROUMANIA. An explanation of the agitation at Bucharest is found in the widely spread belief that King Charles has con- cluded a Convention by which the Roumanian army is placed at the disposal of Austria in, the event of war breaking out with Russia. A despatch from Bucharest states that at the recent greAt meeting the resigna- tion of M. Bratiano was loudly clamoured for. A dele- gate of the assemblage was appointed to go and speak with the King,
' DEATH OF THE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON.

It is with regret that we record the death of the Rev. William Quekett, Rectorof Warrington, which occurred yesterday morning, at the Rectory, in Church-street. The deceased gentleman was in his eighty-sixth year, and had fora long time bell' in failing health. Indeed, his condition had several times recently been very critical, and thus his. de- mise, although it came with something of a shock upon the inhabitants, was not altogether unexpected. Very few people knew of the sad event yesterday„ before morning service, but on the conclusion of service at the Parish Church, the curate, the Rev. J. 4. Drummond, told those there assembled that the painful duty devolved upon him to announce to them the death of the li.ector of Warrington. The REctor, he said, _had passed away that morning, and had finished an earthly pilgrimage of nearly eighty- six years. He had left this world of toil and care, and.gone to that land whence there was no return- ing. He therefore desired the congregation to stand while the organist played the Dead March in "Saul." Directly after this had been done, the service was brought to a conclusion no sermon being preached, and the congregation, many of whom were deeply affected,' then departed. Later in the day, the news of the reverend gentleman' death became generally known throughout the town and neighbourhood, and made a deep impression. . The deceased gentle- man Was up to the time of his death under the care of br. White and Dr. Adams. • The living, which- is.in the gift •of Lord Lilford, is valued at £1,309 per annum; •

FRODSHAM. SERVICE or Sows.—On Monday evening a service of song, entitled •-" Her Benny," was given on .the'Untted Methodist Free Church, Frodsham, by the choir • a`nd friends. • The connective readings were given by the Rev. W. It: Mullett. There-was a good attendance. Mr. H. Aston presided at the harmonium with his accustomed efficiency. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVENENT CLASS.—In connec- tion with this class, a lecture was delivered by Mr. R. Holland, of Frodsham, in the Trinity. School-room, Frodshani, entitled "The Spring: Phenomena of Plant Life." A hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Holland was passed for his excellent and instructiv& lecture. FRODSHAM AIMITRODSHAH LOVIDSRAI. PAROCHIAL COM- mirrEE.—At the monthly meeting el this committee Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., in the chair, the Inspector produced plans of the huts which it is proposed to erect on Prod- sham Marsh for the workmen who will shortly be en- gaged on the Frodsham section of the Manchester Ship Canal. After some discussion it was decided to approve of the plans as being for temporary dwellings, subject to the water supply and drainage arrangements being satis- factorily carried out in accordance with the committee's bye-laws and the-stipplying of another set of plans. This being the last Meeting of the committee for the session, a vote of 'thanks was given to Mr..Thonaas for his services as Chairman during the year. WIFE MAINTENANCE.—At EddisburyTetty Sessions, on Monday, Edwin Holland, a bricklayer, of Overtbn, was summoned by his wife for deserting and refusing to maintain her. Prosecutrix said she hgd been married to the defendant for 2,£.1 years. About three years ago he deserted her, and for the last tWo years and three months of that time she had been in the' Prescot Union. She had three children but two were able to keep themselves. The other, aged seven years, had had to be kept by a relative. Her 'husband had refused either to do anything towards her keep or her child's, although he had good work. Defendant was ordered to pay 8s a week towards his wife's support. He replied that he would not pay a farthing. THE MARGAEINE ACT.—On Monday, at Eddisbury Petty Sessions Martha Jackson, shopkeeper, Frodsham, 'was summoned for having, on the 2nd inst., sold margarine which Was not properly labelled. Superintendent Naylor said he 'visited the defendant's shop on the day named, and asked for a pound of that butter, pointing to something of tilk nature of butter on a connter. The defendant said it was margarine. The Act stated that thereihould be on the margarine a label in capital letters of nig less than 1.1 inches deep, but there was no such label on the margarine in the defendant's shop. The de- fendant, however, did wrap the material ,up in a paper which was marked margarine.—Defendant, who said she thought she Was doing ,right, was fined is and costa, 20s 6th

EXECUTION OF ANOTHER MURDERER.—George Clark was executed at eight o'clock on Tuesday morning at Winchester. He had been vtry penitent since his convic- tion, and paid the greatest attention to the ministrations of the chaplain. Berry gave him a drop of six feet, and death was instantaneous. The body was cut down after hanging an hour. Clark was a discharged soldier and iSublican, of Aldershot, and the crime for which he suf - f ered the death penalty was the murder of Annie Vaughan, his stepdaughter.
